articles.title: The Reading Method That Works
articles.summary: 自然拼读帮助儿童把字母和声音联系起来，但阅读还需要词汇、理解和兴趣。单一方法不能解决所有阅读问题。
articles.text:
Few responsibilities a school carries weigh more heavily than teaching a child to read, and few have provoked so protracted a dispute about method. Phonics, which makes the relationship between letters and sounds explicit, occupies one camp; approaches that immerse children in stories and context occupy the other. For decades the argument has been staged as a contest that one side must win, with curriculum guides, teacher training and test results enlisted on either side.

The evidence, gathered across many classrooms and several decades, now points firmly toward systematic phonics as an indispensable part of early instruction, provided that systematic means taught in a planned sequence rather than picked up incidentally. Children taught how sounds map onto letters decode unfamiliar words with greater confidence, an advantage that matters most to those who struggle from the start; to withhold that code, however rich the surrounding literature, is to ask them to guess. For a child whose home offers few books, school may be the only place where the code is taught at all.

Yet phonics alone has never been enough, and the belief that it might be has done damage of its own. Reading also requires vocabulary, comprehension and motivation, each of which is acquired slowly and largely through use. A child who can sound out a word but does not know what it means has mastered a technique, not a language. Vocabulary grows by hearing and reading words in context, comprehension by discussing what a text assumes, motivation by meeting books that seem to be about one's own life. Conversation, wide reading and unhurried practice supply what no worksheet can, and they take time that crowded timetables rarely allow.

Framed as a war between methods, the debate misdescribes what effective classrooms actually do. The strongest teachers combine approaches, using phonics to hand children the code and stories to give them a reason to use it; curiosity, far from being an interruption, is treated as a resource. A method is a tool, not a complete education, and a good reading lesson draws on every tool available, including the child's own interest.

articles.title: The Good Climate News
articles.summary: 气候新闻不全是坏消息。清洁能源成本下降、保护项目见效和技术进步，也值得记录，但不应掩盖排放仍在上升的现实。
articles.text:
Climate reporting tends toward the alarming, and not without cause: temperature records fall, disasters multiply, and targets announced with ceremony are quietly missed. Yet the same period has produced genuine gains. Solar and wind power have become far cheaper than their early advocates dared to predict; some forests and wildlife populations have recovered; electric vehicles have moved from curiosity to commonplace. None of this cancels the damage, but it belongs in the account.

Such news matters, and not merely as relief. It demonstrates that change is possible, which is precisely what despair denies, and it can draw investment and political will toward solutions that have proved themselves. The danger is subtler: a handful of success stories can breed complacency, encouraging the comfortable conclusion that the trend has turned when it has not, and the stories most likely to travel are those that flatter their audience.

Honest reporting holds both truths at once. Emissions remain far too high, and some changes, among them melting ice and failing harvests, are accelerating rather than slowing. At the same time, clean technologies keep improving and some policies are demonstrably working. The difficulty is that the two halves of the picture operate on different timescales: a policy may succeed within a decade while the atmosphere responds over centuries, so a genuine victory and a deepening crisis can be reported in the same week. To present only one half is to misinform, whether the omission flatters optimism or confirms gloom.

The lesson is neither to celebrate nor to despair, but to attend closely to what is actually changing and to demand more from the solutions that work. Progress is real, and it is not yet enough; a realistic hope is built on evidence rather than on ignoring the bad news. The climate story is still being written, and its ending depends on decisions not yet taken.

articles.title: College in the Age of AI
articles.summary: AI 让大学重新思考“学什么、怎么评”。如果只考最终答案，工具会取代思考；重视过程、讨论和判断，才能保住学习。
articles.text:
Universities are being pressed to answer a question they have long avoided: what is a degree for? If it consists mainly in producing correct answers, artificial intelligence can now supply much of the work, and do so faster and more cheaply. If it consists in developing judgement, the capacity to weigh evidence, notice what is missing and decide, then AI is a tool that may help or hinder, depending on how it is used and on what the course asks students to do with it.

Many courses still rest on essays and examinations that measure the final product. AI makes such assessments easier to fake, and the fakery is difficult to detect. Some professors have responded by returning to in-class writing, oral examinations and assignments that require students to explain their process rather than merely display its result. An oral examination, inefficient as it is, at least requires the student to be present in the reasoning.

Redesigning assessment, however, is slower and harder than announcing it. Large classes, limited time and institutional rules constrain what a single instructor can change, and students need clear, consistent guidance; where rules differ from course to course, those who try to follow them are penalised while others proceed unhindered. A policy that punishes honesty, however unintentionally, teaches students that the safest course is to hide their methods.

The deeper issue is purpose. A university should not merely transmit information, of which there is now an abundance, but teach students how to question, compare and decide. AI can support that work by drafting, summarising and challenging, provided that the student remains the one who judges what the machine produces. The habits of attention that reading and argument cultivate cannot be delegated, because they are formed by practice and by being held to account. What AI cannot replace are the relationships and expectations, the seminar, the argument, the professor who notices, that make learning possible in the first place. A degree should certify judgement, not merely production.

articles.title: AI Models Must Adapt
articles.summary: AI 模型更新越来越快，企业需要判断何时升级、何时保留旧系统。成本、可靠性、隐私和依赖风险都要权衡。
articles.text:
AI models improve at a pace that unsettles the organisations which depend on them. Each new version promises better reasoning, longer context and lower cost, and the pressure to upgrade is intense. Yet switching is rarely the simple matter that marketing implies, and the cost of changing one's mind rises with every system built on the last. Nor is the choice easily reversible once code, contracts and staff training have settled around a particular interface.

A model that performs impressively in a demonstration may behave quite differently in production. It may prove more expensive at scale, less reliable on the specific task it was bought for, or harder to integrate with systems built around its predecessor. Data privacy and vendor dependence complicate the calculation further: a company that has rebuilt its workflow around one provider may find, once the costs of migration are counted, that it can no longer leave. Lock-in is seldom the result of a single decision; it accumulates through a hundred small ones, each of which seemed sensible at the time.

The most cautious firms therefore test candidate models on their own tasks before committing, comparing accuracy, latency and cost under realistic conditions. They preserve the ability to switch, even at some inconvenience, and they monitor for drift, since a model that worked last month may behave differently after a silent update. What they are buying, in effect, is not a product but a relationship they intend to be able to end.

Adoption, then, is not a one-time purchase but an ongoing operational choice, one that must be revisited as prices, capabilities and risks shift. The best model is not always the newest; it is the one that fits the work, the budget and the risks a company can actually manage. A model is infrastructure, and good infrastructure is designed to change, not to be permanent.

articles.title: La Niña and the Food Supply
articles.summary: 拉尼娜现象可能扰乱降雨和农作物，影响全球粮食价格。气候风险通过贸易和供应链传导，贫困地区最脆弱。
articles.text:
La Niña is a climate pattern that rearranges rainfall and temperature across the globe, bringing drought to some regions and floods to others. For farmers, the consequences can be severe, and they are rarely confined to the season in which they appear or to the country in which the weather itself was unusual. No single season tells the whole story, which is why forecasters speak of probabilities rather than certainties.

Crops are acutely sensitive to timing. A dry spell during planting, or a flood shortly before harvest, can cut yields sharply; when several major producers are affected at once, global prices rise, and poorer countries, which spend a larger share of household income on food, absorb the blow hardest. Farmers with savings can wait for better prices; those without must sell at whatever the market offers that week.

The effects travel through supply chains rather than through weather alone. A failed harvest in one country may raise prices in another, while shipping costs, storage capacity and trade policy determine how quickly the shock reaches consumers. Trade restrictions imposed in a panic can amplify the very shortage they were meant to address. Climate risk, in other words, is never merely a local meteorological problem; it is economic and political at the same time, and it is distributed unequally, falling hardest on those who contributed least to the emissions that drive it.

Adaptation can help. Drought-resistant crops, better irrigation, early warning systems and social protection for farmers all soften the impact, and each has been shown to work somewhere. But adaptation has limits, and without reductions in emissions the frequency and intensity of such shocks are likely to increase, overwhelming the capacity of even well-designed systems to absorb them. Rich countries can build reservoirs and import shortfalls; poorer ones often cannot. The weather is not fair; policy can at least be.

articles.title: Strength After 50
articles.summary: 年龄增长会流失肌肉，但力量训练仍有效。从轻负荷开始、循序渐进，能改善平衡、日常活动和独立生活。
articles.text:
Muscle loss is a normal accompaniment of ageing, but it is not something people must accept without resistance. After fifty, adults lose muscle mass and strength more quickly, and the consequences show up in ordinary life: walking becomes slower, balance less secure, and carrying shopping or rising from a chair turns into an effort easily mistaken for a passing weakness. Frailty, once it sets in, is far harder to reverse than to prevent.

Strength training can slow the process, and it does not require a gym or heavy weights. Resistance bands, body-weight exercises, bottles of water and the simple act of climbing stairs all provide a sufficient challenge, since the body responds to effort rather than to equipment. Short, regular sessions are enough to begin, and consistency matters more than ambition. Encouragement matters as much as instruction, since many older adults assume that strength training belongs to a younger generation and that a gym membership is the price of admission. The key is to start at a manageable level and to increase gradually, so that the body adapts rather than rebels.

For older adults the benefits are practical rather than athletic. Stronger legs reduce the risk of falls, which remain among the most serious threats to independence, while stronger arms make daily tasks easier. Equally important is what training prevents: the fall that ends independent living often begins with a leg that could not recover its balance. Training also supports bone health and mood, and a doctor or instructor can help those with health conditions to adapt the exercises safely.

It is never too late to begin, and the goal is not to become an athlete but to keep doing the things that make life independent and enjoyable. Strength, on this view, is not a luxury reserved for the young; it is part of what allows people to live on their own terms for longer, and capability rewards patience more than intensity.

articles.title: What Learning Really Is
articles.summary: 学习不只是记忆和考试。阅读、提问和想象别人的生活，能培养同理心和判断力，这些是分数无法完全衡量的。
articles.text:
Learning is usually measured by tests. A student memorises facts, answers questions and receives a score, and the score is taken to stand for the learning. Yet much of what matters most is difficult to measure in this way, and some of it never appears on a transcript at all. Scores are convenient, comparable and cheap to produce, which explains their influence as much as their accuracy does.

Reading a story can help a student imagine a life very different from their own; a history lesson can show how choices made long ago still shape the present; a discussion can teach someone to listen, to disagree without hostility and to change their mind when the argument warrants it. Each of these asks the student to hold two perspectives at once, a habit that no examination easily captures. None of the experiences reliably produces a higher score the following week, and none of them is wasted for that reason.

What they produce may take years to surface in a person's decisions, and it is precisely for that reason that they are easily neglected when budgets tighten. A society needs people who can understand others, question authority and think beyond the obvious answer, capacities that no multiple-choice item captures and that a curriculum organised around examination performance tends to crowd out. What is measured expands; what is not measured quietly disappears from the timetable.

Exams have their place. They check knowledge, expose gaps and give feedback that neither teacher nor student could otherwise obtain. But they are not the whole of education, and a school that confuses the two will produce students who are good at being tested and uncertain how to learn. The deepest learning often begins with a question rather than an answer, and a good education leaves a person able to keep learning long after the test is over. A test is not the enemy of learning; a test that ignores learning is.

articles.title: The Business of Books
articles.summary: 商业书籍市场繁荣，但质量参差。读者需要区分可靠研究与流行口号，出版社和评论者也承担筛选责任。
articles.text:
Business books form a large and profitable market. Each year thousands of titles promise better leadership, higher productivity and a clearer strategy, and each arrives with a cover, a slogan and an author whose confidence rarely falters. Publishing rewards writers who can turn a single insight into a system; readers, for their part, tend to prefer confidence to doubt.

The result is a paradox. There has never been more access to ideas about management, yet it has never been harder to know which of them are reliable. A book can become influential because it is well marketed rather than because its evidence is strong, and the two are not always easy to distinguish from the outside: the prose is polished in both cases, and the case studies are equally vivid. The market filters for memorability, not accuracy, and the two are only loosely connected.

Readers can protect themselves by asking a few pointed questions. What is the evidence? Who, precisely, was studied, and over what period? Does the author acknowledge failure and uncertainty, or does every anecdote resolve into a lesson? The questions are simple, but asking them takes a discipline the genre actively discourages. A good business book should offer more than a feeling of inspiration; it should help a reader think, and it should be willing to describe the cases that did not work, since a method that succeeds everywhere has probably been tested nowhere.

Publishers and reviewers carry a share of the responsibility. Serious editing, fact-checking and honest criticism separate useful ideas from fashionable ones, and a market that rewards speed over scrutiny will keep producing confident books with thin foundations. Reviewers, in particular, are poorly paid and easily flattered by access to authors. In so crowded a field the scarcest resource is not information, of which there is plenty, but judgement.

articles.title: Exams in the Age of AI
articles.summary: AI 让传统考试更难验证真实学习。学校需要重新设计评价方式，重视过程、口头表达和课堂表现，而不仅是最终答案。
articles.text:
AI has made it far easier to produce a polished essay, a correct answer or a convincing summary. For schools, this raises an awkward question that predates the technology but can no longer be postponed: what does an examination actually measure? The question is old, but the urgency is new.

Where the task is to recall facts, AI can help a student cheat; where it is to solve a problem, AI can produce the solution without the student understanding it. Where the task is to summarise a source, AI can produce a summary that is fluent and accurate in detail yet entirely detached from the reading it claims to represent. Traditional examinations were always imperfect proxies for learning, but AI widens the gap between performance and understanding until it becomes impossible to ignore. A student can now submit work better than anything they could have written, and learn nothing in the process.

Some schools are responding by changing what they assess. In-class writing, oral examinations, presentations and process portfolios take more time and are harder to standardise, yet they reveal how a student thinks rather than merely what a student produces. Teachers report that such formats are more exhausting to mark and more revealing to read. The point is not to make examinations harder for its own sake, but to make them meaningful, which means accepting that some of what is worth testing cannot be scored by a machine.

An examination should show what a student can do without a machine as well as what they can do with one; both matter, and they are not the same competence. A school that tests only the final product will remain permanently vulnerable to whatever tool produces it best, and the future of assessment will depend on what schools decide learning is for. A machine can answer; a student must learn why the answer matters.

articles.title: The Productivity Promise
articles.summary: 生成式 AI 可能节省工作时间，但节省的时间是否变成休息或更高产出，取决于管理和分配。
articles.text:
A recent report suggests that AI tools can save workers nearly an hour a day. The finding is striking, and companies in search of efficiency have welcomed it; but saving time is not the same thing as improving work, and the difference is not technical. Such figures circulate because they are easy to repeat and hard to verify, which is itself a lesson about productivity research.

If the saved hour is quietly filled with additional tasks, the worker may end the day busier without being better off. If it is used to shorten hours, raise quality or protect health, the benefit is real. Which of these happens depends less on the software than on how managers measure success and what they are rewarded for; a system that counts output will absorb every saving it is given. A team that finishes early is often rewarded with more work, which teaches everyone to appear busy instead.

There is also a question of distribution. Productivity gains may raise profits while wages stay flat, and workers may be expected to produce more within the same hours rather than share in what their output earns. Without negotiation and regulation, the benefits of efficiency tend to concentrate at the top of the organisation, where decisions about workload are made and where the gains are most easily recorded. The gains are real, but their destination is a matter of bargaining power rather than of engineering.

AI can be a genuinely useful tool, but the promise of less work is not automatic. It requires deliberate choices about workload, pay and time, and those choices are made by institutions rather than by algorithms. Technology can save an hour; what happens to that hour is a decision someone must take, and whether it is taken deliberately or by default determines almost everything about whether the technology improves working life or merely intensifies it.

articles.title: AI Goes to School
articles.summary: AI 进入课堂后，学校在“禁止”和“放开”之间寻找规则。关键不是工具本身，而是它是否帮助学生思考。
articles.text:
Walk into almost any well-resourced secondary school and you will find, somewhere on the timetable, a task that a language model could complete in under a minute. Students ask such systems to explain a difficult concept, to rehearse a foreign language or to comment on a draft; teachers use them to sketch lesson plans and to generate worked examples. Adoption, in other words, has run well ahead of policy, and the gap is widening.

School responses have divided accordingly. A minority prohibit the technology outright, others permit it for specified tasks, and a great many have yet to decide. Framing the dispute as a contest between honesty and dishonesty, however, misstates what is at stake. Cheating is a genuine concern, but the deeper question is what learning should look like once a machine can produce a polished answer in seconds. Rules drafted in a hurry tend either to forbid behaviour that is already widespread or to license uses that nobody has thought through.

A more defensible rule is to begin with the intended learning. Where the aim is to practise grammar or to memorise vocabulary, a model can act as a tireless partner, offering correction at any hour. Where the aim is to construct an argument, by contrast, delegating the first draft may remove precisely the struggle through which the skill is acquired. The instrument itself is neither benign nor corrupt; its value is conferred by the purpose to which it is put.

That distinction places a new obligation on schools. Students need to learn to use these systems critically: verifying claims, recognising bias and being able to explain what they themselves contributed. A school that ignores the technology risks sending students into the world unprepared, while one that adopts it uncritically may erode the very learning it exists to protect. The question, finally, is not whether students will use AI, but what they will learn when they do.

Nowhere is the arithmetic of a warming planet more visible than in the far north. The Arctic is heating faster than almost any other region, and its frozen ground, known as permafrost, holds an immense stock of carbon accumulated over millennia from plants and animals that never fully decayed. As temperatures rise and the ground thaws, microbes resume the work that the cold suspended, releasing carbon dioxide and, where the soil is waterlogged, methane.

Scientists sometimes call this a carbon bomb. The metaphor is arresting, though it misleads if taken literally: what is stored will not detonate in a single season. The release is gradual, unfolding over decades, and its pace depends on how far the planet warms and how quickly the ice-rich layers give way. Yet gradualism offers no comfort. Methane traps heat far more effectively than carbon dioxide over the short term, and the emissions released by thawing feed back into the warming that caused them, so that each increment of temperature invites the next.

The consequences are local as well as atmospheric. Ground that once stayed solid for most of the year softens beneath roads, buildings and pipelines, undermining infrastructure on which northern communities depend and forcing costly, improvised repairs. For people already living at the edge of the habitable, the thaw is not a projection but a recurring disruption, arriving earlier each spring and retreating later each autumn.

Cutting global emissions remains the only means of limiting the risk at its source, since no local measure can offset the warming that drives the process. There is, besides, a lag built into the system: even a sharp fall in emissions would leave the carbon already stored in the ground responding to the warmth accumulated so far. Monitoring permafrost and helping northern communities adapt are therefore essential, both to anticipate sudden collapse and to protect those with the fewest means of moving. The Arctic, it turns out, is not a distant wilderness but a component of the climate system on which everyone depends.

Technology is usually reported as a sequence of launches: a new device, a new model, a new feature, each with a date and a price. The shifts that matter most, however, are institutional rather than technical — who controls the data, who writes the rules, who absorbs the risk when something goes wrong — and these rarely arrive with a press release. A launch announces a product; an institutional change redistributes power, which is why the second is so much harder to photograph.

Artificial intelligence dominated the year. Having escaped the laboratory, it turned up in workplaces, classrooms and public services, and the argument around it changed character: the question was no longer what the technology could do but how it ought to be governed. Copyright, bias, energy consumption and the displacement of labour moved from specialist journals into ordinary conversation, and regulators who had spent a decade chasing social media found themselves, once again, behind.

Platform regulation advanced in parallel. Governments pressed companies to explain how their algorithms ranked content, to shield children from the worst of it and to open their data to independent researchers. Results varied widely and enforcement was uneven, yet the underlying principle became harder to deny: a platform is not a neutral pipe through which other people's speech flows. By deciding what is amplified and what is buried, it shapes what its users see, and it does so continuously and invisibly.

Digital politics supplied a third strand. Elections, misinformation and online organising showed how quickly a technical change can rearrange public life, and how poorly existing institutions anticipate it. Taken together, the year's trends suggest that no technology story is ever purely technical; each is an argument about power, and none of those arguments has been settled. New products will keep arriving on schedule. The disputes they provoke will not be resolved by a launch.

articles.title: The Century of Solitude
articles.summary: 现代社会的独处时间增加，社区联系减少。便利、住房和工作方式改变了社交，孤独成为公共问题而非私人失败。
articles.text:
Solitude has become, for many people, the default condition of daily life, and the reasons are largely architectural and economic rather than temperamental. Homes are larger, so there is less need to go out for space; shopping is online, so there is less need to go out for goods; work can be done remotely, so there is less need to go out for company; entertainment arrives on demand, so there is less need to go out at all. Each convenience quietly removes a reason to depend on a neighbour.

The resulting life is quieter and more private, and for some people it is a genuine gain. Privacy is not a pathology, and the ability to withdraw is one of the freedoms a wealthy society affords. For others, the same conditions curdle into isolation. Contact that once occurred by accident, in a lift or at a bus stop or over a garden fence, now has to be arranged in advance; what was a background hum of acquaintance has become a scheduling problem, and friendship demands an effort that crowded calendars rarely permit.

Loneliness, moreover, is not merely a private sorrow. It is associated with poorer health, lower trust and weaker communities, and it tends to compound itself: those who are isolated find it harder to ask for help, while neighbourhoods that have lost their shared spaces find it harder to notice that help is needed. The burden falls unevenly, since the old, the poor and the recently arrived have the thinnest networks to begin with.

None of this can be cured by nostalgia, nor by pretending that earlier social arrangements were kinder than they were. What is required is deliberate design: public spaces worth lingering in, community institutions with stable funding, neighbourhoods that mix housing with workplaces and shops, and recurring rituals that give people a reason to assemble. A society that has made it easy to stay at home must now make it just as easy to go out.

articles.title: What AI Can't Do in Class
articles.summary: AI 能生成答案，却不能替代教师的判断、关系和责任。学校应把 AI 当助手，保留人的监督和学生的思考过程。
articles.text:
Ask a modern language model to write an essay, solve an equation or explain a concept in three languages and it will comply in seconds. The performance is genuinely impressive, and schools are right to take it seriously rather than hope it goes away. Impressive, however, is not the same as sufficient, and the abilities on display do not displace everything a teacher does.

Consider what a teacher notices. She sees the student who has been staring at the same paragraph for ten minutes, the one who is tired, the one who is nodding in order to conceal incomprehension; she knows which family is under strain and which topic will land badly on a Monday morning; she can abandon a lesson plan halfway through when the room has not understood. These are acts of judgement, formed through years of contact with actual students, and no model surveying text has access to the evidence on which they rest.

Responsibility is a further gap. When a tool returns a wrong answer it cannot be held to account; the school, the teacher and the designer can be, and someone must be. That is why human oversight remains indispensable in assessment and feedback, where an error does not merely inconvenience but misdirects a student's understanding and, eventually, their prospects.

The sensible conclusion is not that AI should be kept out of classrooms, still less that it should replace the people in them. It is that the technology should absorb the repetitive work — practice drills, instant corrections, translations — and release teachers for what only a person can supply: discussion, encouragement, challenge and care. A program can let a student rehearse; it cannot mind whether that student succeeds. A school that treats itself as a content delivery system has already conceded the argument it thinks it is winning.

articles.title: Trees in the City
articles.summary: 城市种树不仅美化街道，也能降温、改善空气、支持心理健康。但种下之后需要长期养护，否则树苗很难长大。
articles.text:
Cities have discovered trees, and they are planting them in numbers that would have seemed implausible a generation ago. The motives are practical: shade in summer, streets that stay cooler than the surrounding suburbs, air carrying less particulate matter, and somewhere for birds and insects to live. In dense neighbourhoods that possess almost no green space, the effect on mental well-being is now counted among the benefits rather than treated as a pleasant by-product.

Planting, however, is the easy part. A young tree needs water through its first summers, protection from vehicles and vandalism, and soil that has not been compacted by construction machinery. Set into a narrow pit, surrounded by paving and starved of moisture, a sapling may survive for years without ever growing, and many die before they deliver any of the benefits their planting was meant to secure.

Placement and species matter as much as aftercare. A tree chosen for the climate and soil it will actually meet stands a chance; one selected for how it looks in a catalogue does not. Nor should trees go where roots will crack pipes or branches will block a sightline, since the resulting complaints can turn a council against planting altogether. Residents, meanwhile, can do more than admire: watering during dry spells, reporting damage and defending trees during roadworks are forms of maintenance that no department can supply on its own.

The difficulty is one of timescales. A mature tree offers shade, cleaner air and cooler streets on a scale no sapling can match, yet those benefits accrue over decades while the costs of planting and watering fall due immediately. A city that plants for a photograph is not the same as a city that plans for shade in twenty years, and only the second is making an investment rather than a gesture.

articles.title: The Dopamine Trap
articles.summary: 手机应用利用奖励机制吸引注意力。理解通知、点赞和无限滚动如何影响大脑，有助于重新掌握使用习惯。
articles.text:
Few objects in ordinary life are as carefully engineered to resist being put down as a smartphone. Notifications arrive at intervals calculated to interrupt; likes accumulate in quantities just large enough to be flattering; short videos end before boredom can take hold. None of this is accidental. It is the output of teams employed for the specific purpose of keeping attention where it is.

The mechanism exploits an old feature of the brain's reward system, which responds most strongly not to certainties but to novelty and uncertainty. A message may be tedious or thrilling, a video hilarious or dull; the point is that the user cannot tell until the next tap. This is what researchers call a variable reward, and it is the same principle that makes a slot machine so difficult to leave. The device is not addictive in any clinical sense, and the comparison with gambling is imperfect, but the design logic behind both is uncomfortably similar.

Companies have commercial reasons for building such mechanisms into their products, since time spent inside an app converts into advertising revenue and into detailed data about behaviour. Users typically experience their choices as free, and in a narrow sense they are. But an environment engineered to make one option frictionless and the alternatives effortful is not a neutral one, and the preferences it produces are partly its own creation.

Understanding the design is the first step towards resisting it. Non-essential notifications can be switched off, the most compulsive apps moved off the home screen or deleted, and checking confined to specified times rather than performed whenever a device demands attention. The objective is not to renounce the technology, which would be neither possible nor desirable, but to decide deliberately when and how it is allowed to claim attention. Willpower, treated as a private virtue, is a thin defence against an environment designed by specialists; it works better when the environment itself is rearranged.

articles.title: A New Era of Hunger
articles.summary: 饥饿问题并未消失，而是以新的形式出现。冲突、气候冲击、贫困和不平等让食物不安全加剧，需要长期政策而非短期援助。
articles.text:
Hunger is generally imagined as a relic of the past or as a catastrophe confined to distant places, and both assumptions are wrong. Food insecurity is rising in many countries, including wealthy ones, and its causes are not primarily a shortage of food. Conflict, climate shocks, poverty, insecure work and thin social protection all push households towards the edge, and once there a single bad month, whether an illness or a rent increase or a broken car, is enough to tip them over.

Food banks and emergency aid do necessary work, and it would be callous to disparage them. They are, nevertheless, a response to failure rather than a remedy for it. What households need is a stable income, housing they can afford and reasonable access to healthy food; schools, health services and local markets each have a part to play in providing it, and none can substitute for the others.

The politics of the subject are unavoidable. Food is rarely scarce in the literal sense; it is frequently unaffordable, or badly distributed, or wasted in one place while people go without in another. A country can discard edible produce in the same week that its citizens queue at a donation point, and no amount of charitable effort will close that gap. Closing it requires decisions about wages, prices, land use and social security, decisions that are political by nature and are often presented as merely technical.

The lesson is that hunger is not a natural disaster to which governments can do no more than respond. It is a consequence of choices, and those choices can be made differently. A society that treats food as a basic right will set different priorities from one that treats it as a commodity to be bought and sold, and the difference will show up not in speeches but in the number of children who arrive at school having already eaten.

articles.title: The Anti-Social Century
articles.summary: 现代生活让人更容易独处。居住、工作、消费和娱乐方式的变化减少了偶然社交，而友谊和社区需要重复接触。
articles.text:
Americans now spend more of their waking hours alone than at any point for which records exist, and the explanation is not that they have become more introverted. The change is embedded in the ordinary arrangements of life: houses built further apart, commutes that consume the evening, shopping conducted by screen, work performed from a spare bedroom, entertainment delivered on demand. Each of these is a convenience, and each removes an occasion on which a stranger might have become an acquaintance.

The loss is cumulative because friendship rarely begins with an introduction. It begins with repetition: the same cafe at the same hour, the same gym, the same gate at school pickup, the same bus stop in the rain. Low-pressure repetition is what allows people to recognise one another, to exchange remarks, and eventually to rely on one another. Where such settings are missing, relationships do not so much fail as never start, and the absence is hard to notice because nothing has visibly broken.

The consequences are both personal and civic. Loneliness is associated with poorer health, and communities whose members rarely encounter one another are less able to organise around shared problems, whether a failing school, a closing surgery or a road that needs fixing. A society composed of private comforts can drift into being a society of strangers, well provided for and thinly connected.

The remedy is not to renounce convenience, which nobody would accept, but to rebuild the settings in which unplanned meeting is possible: parks that invite people to stay, libraries that admit anyone, clubs with modest subscriptions, markets, festivals and streets designed so that walking is pleasant rather than merely permitted. Connection of that kind has to be built into the physical and institutional fabric of a place. It cannot be wished into existence, and it will not survive on sentiment alone.

articles.title: The Air We Share
articles.summary: 空气污染影响全球数十亿人，室内外污染都与疾病和早逝相关。清洁能源、交通转型和家庭燃料改善是重点。
articles.text:
Among environmental risks to health, air pollution is one of the most widespread and the least dramatised. It contributes to heart disease, stroke, lung cancer and respiratory infection, and the World Health Organization estimates that millions of premature deaths each year are linked to polluted air. Unlike a factory fire or an oil spill, it has no single author and no memorable photograph; the damage is inflicted in the ordinary course of breathing, which is precisely what makes it so easy to overlook.

Sources differ by setting. Outdoors, the principal contributors are traffic, industry, power generation and the open burning of waste; indoors, they are cooking stoves, heating and inadequate ventilation. The two are often treated as separate problems, yet in many low-income households they are the same problem experienced in sequence: smoke from a stove in the morning, exhaust from the road outside the window at night, with no clean interval between. For those households, indoor air can be fully as dangerous as the air outside.

The remedies are known and, in principle, affordable. Cleaner energy, reliable public transport, stricter vehicle standards and improved cooking technologies all reduce exposure, as does urban planning that keeps industry away from homes and provides green space where people actually live. Enforcement matters as much as ambition, since a standard that is never monitored is little more than a statement of intent. The case for acting is economic as well as medical: illness and lost productivity are expensive, and the costs fall hardest on the health systems least able to absorb them.

The difficulty is political. Pollution crosses borders, and it harms people who contributed least to it and who have the fewest means of avoiding it. No municipality, however diligent, can clean its air through its own efforts alone, and a response confined to local action will always be incomplete. Clean air is a shared resource, and it can be protected only by arrangements that treat it as one.

articles.title: The Fitness Reset
articles.summary: 开始运动不必一次改变全部生活。设定小目标、安排固定时间、找到喜欢的活动，比依赖意志力更容易坚持。
articles.text:
Every January, gyms fill with people who have resolved to change their lives, and by February many of the same people have quietly abandoned the plan they were so confident about. It is tempting to blame a lack of willpower, but the more plausible explanation lies in design. A routine that demands an unfamiliar schedule, expensive equipment and flawless time management is, from the outset, a routine built to collapse at the first busy week.

What succeeds instead is far less dramatic. Ten minutes of walking, a short strength session or a handful of stretches, performed consistently, can establish the habit on which everything else depends. Consistency rather than intensity is the variable that matters early on, because a habit that already exists is much easier to extend than one that has never taken root. Beginners who attempt too much too quickly tend to mistake exhaustion for progress and to quit just before the benefits would have appeared.

Equally important is choosing an activity that is genuinely enjoyed. Where the gym feels like a punishment to be endured, a dance class, a bicycle ride or a walk taken with a friend may prove more durable, since pleasure is a more reliable motivator than guilt. Treating exercise as an appointment, entered in a calendar and defended like any other commitment, further protects it from becoming the first thing sacrificed when a day grows crowded.

Missing a day, meanwhile, should not be read as failure. The useful question is not why the streak was broken but what would make the next session easier to begin. Nor should an interrupted week be taken as proof that the effort was wasted, since what matters is whether the habit resumes, not whether it was ever interrupted. A plan that survives a bad week, however modest it looks on paper, is worth more than an ambitious one that does not survive at all. Movement, in the end, has to fit the life a person actually leads rather than the one they imagine they ought to lead.

articles.title: Learning to Fail
articles.summary: 失败不是学习的反面，而是学习的一部分。允许试错、复盘和重新尝试，能帮助学生建立韧性，而不是只追求完美成绩。
articles.text:
From the earliest years of schooling, students absorb a simple lesson: mistakes are costly. A wrong answer lowers a grade, and a failed examination comes to feel less like an event than a verdict on character. Over time the lesson takes hold, and otherwise capable students begin to avoid any task at which they might not immediately excel, which is to say they avoid the tasks from which they would learn most.

Yet error is not the opposite of learning; it is one of its mechanisms. A child who never struggles never discovers how to recover, and a student who fails, reflects and tries again acquires something a flawless record cannot supply: resilience, resourcefulness and a more honest estimate of their own abilities. Error, after all, is information, since it indicates precisely where understanding is incomplete, something a correct answer never does. What damages learners is not failure itself but failure that is never examined, because an unexplained mistake is simply repeated in a different form.

Teachers therefore have considerable influence over whether failure instructs or merely wounds. Feedback that names what went wrong, opportunities to revise and resubmit, and a classroom in which questions are welcomed rather than tolerated all make the risk of trying feel bearable. So does a distinction that adults often forget to make aloud: a poor piece of work is not evidence of a poor person, and students who confuse the two grow defensive precisely when they most need to be curious.

None of this means that failure is valuable merely because it hurts. It becomes valuable only when it is reflected upon and put to use. The aim is neither to celebrate mistakes nor to lower expectations until nobody can fail, but to make error a stage in learning rather than its conclusion. A mistake can be a lesson or a judgement, and what separates the two is almost always what happens next.

articles.title: A Better Way to Think About AI
articles.summary: AI 不只是替代工作，也会改变任务组合。政策应关注工人能否获得新技能、谈判力量和社会保障，而不是只预测岗位数量。
articles.text:
Much of the public conversation about artificial intelligence revolves around a single question: how many jobs will disappear? The question is understandable, and it is not trivial, but it is framed in a way that obscures more than it reveals. Technology seldom abolishes an entire occupation in one stroke; far more often it redistributes the tasks of which that occupation is composed.

Consider two familiar examples. A radiologist may spend less time reading routine scans and more time consulting with patients, explaining results and weighing uncertain findings, while a customer service worker may field fewer simple queries and handle a larger share of complicated complaints. The job survives, but its centre of gravity shifts, and the skills that once guaranteed competence may no longer be the ones in demand. Some workers make that adjustment easily, drawing on training and confidence they already possess; others need support that no market, left to itself, is likely to supply.

How the gains are distributed matters as much as how large they are. If AI raises productivity while the benefits accrue mainly to owners of capital, workers may feel worse off even as output climbs, and the political consequences of that perception are rarely mild. If the same gains are shared, through higher wages, shorter hours or better public services, the identical technology can improve ordinary lives. Distribution, in other words, is not an afterthought to innovation; it is part of what innovation turns out to mean.

Policy, then, should concentrate on transitions rather than predictions. Forecasting which occupations will vanish is a precarious business; equipping people to move into new tasks is not. Training that employers and workers both recognise, benefits that travel between jobs, collective bargaining and a sturdier social safety net all make the passage less punishing. The future of work will not be decided by the technology alone. It will be decided by institutions, and by whether those institutions treat adjustment as a shared cost or a private misfortune.

articles.title: Can AI Be Trusted in Schools?

articles.text:
Schools are adopting artificial intelligence faster than they can evaluate it. Tools now tutor students through exercises, grade essays and flag learners who appear to be falling behind, and the promises attached to them are genuinely attractive: personalised practice, less administrative drudgery and feedback delivered in seconds rather than weeks. Budgets are committed and pilots launched long before anyone has defined what improvement would look like, and few institutions wish to be left behind.

That evidence, when it arrives, remains mixed. AI can supply repeated practice with immediate correction, which suits students who need rehearsal, and it can relieve teachers of routine marking. But the quality of such tools varies enormously, their errors are frequently plausible enough to escape notice, and a system trained on biased data will reproduce unfair patterns with perfect consistency. A wrong answer delivered confidently is harder to challenge than one delivered hesitantly, and students are not always equipped to tell the difference. Nor is a tool's popularity evidence of its value, since adoption and effectiveness are separate questions that are easily confused.

Teachers, for their part, remain indispensable. They read a room, notice confusion before it hardens into failure, and make contextual judgements that no model can make on their behalf. The most promising uses of AI treat it as an assistant rather than an authority: something that prepares materials, suggests explanations and absorbs repetition, while the human being retains responsibility for what is taught and why. Students, similarly, must still be asked to explain their reasoning and to question what a machine returns.

The real question is therefore not whether AI belongs in schools, since it is already there, but what schools want it to accomplish. Adopted without a clear purpose, technology can add cost and complexity while improving very little. Trust is built by evidence rather than enthusiasm, and the answer will depend on the purpose, the evidence and the people who remain accountable when something goes wrong.

articles.title: What Professors Do With AI

Artificial intelligence in higher education is usually discussed as a student problem: cheating, shortcuts, and essays that nobody in the room actually wrote. Yet professors are users too. They draft examination questions with it, ask it to explain a stubborn concept in simpler terms, condense readings before a seminar, and generate preliminary feedback on student drafts.

A recent survey suggests that such use is growing but distinctly uneven. Some faculty deploy AI for routine tasks and then check the output line by line, treating it as a fast but unreliable assistant. Others avoid it altogether, citing concerns about accuracy, privacy and academic standards. Perhaps the largest group sits somewhere in between, uncertain what their institution permits and reluctant to ask, since admitting to use may invite suspicion. Ambiguity of that kind is not resolved by silence; it is merely displaced onto students, who receive advice of wildly inconsistent quality depending on which office they happen to enter.

The risks are not hypothetical. AI can invent sources that look authoritative, reproduce the biases embedded in its training data, and produce feedback that sounds confident while being simply wrong. Students may have no way of knowing whether a comment on their essay came from a person or a machine, and trust, already fragile, suffers when that ambiguity is left unaddressed. Saving time, moreover, is not the same as improving learning; a tool can shorten a task while quietly degrading the judgement the task was meant to develop.

What the moment calls for is neither a blanket ban nor a free-for-all, but clear guidance, serious training and an ingrained habit of verification. Institutions owe their staff explicit rules and the time to learn what the tools can and cannot do. Yet even the best-governed use of AI leaves one thing unchanged: a tool can save labour, but it cannot take responsibility. That remains with the people who teach, and with the classroom that they, rather than the software, define.

articles.title: How to Be a Better Friend

Friendship is often treated as something that happens to people rather than something they do. In childhood it is largely a matter of proximity: friends are whoever shares the same class or the same street. In adulthood the assumption survives, even though the conditions that once made it true have vanished, and relationships that neither party intended to lose are gradually eroded by work, family and distance. The erosion is rarely noticed at the time, because no single week contains a rupture; there is only a slow accumulation of postponed calls.

What sustains them is rarely dramatic. A message on a birthday, a call at the end of a difficult week, a note referring to something the other person mentioned months ago: none of these is remarkable in itself, yet each carries the same quiet message, that one was remembered and has not been forgotten. Listening belongs to the same category. Rushing to offer solutions can be a way of ending a conversation about difficulty, whereas what is often needed is not a remedy but a witness, someone willing to hear the account without immediately attempting to correct it.

Honesty matters as much as attention. Good friends disagree, apologise and repair, and they manage this without keeping a ledger of favours given and received, which would turn generosity into debt. They also allow for change, including the possibility that one person will have less time or energy for a season, without reading that temporary absence as rejection. A friendship too rigid to accommodate a bad year is unlikely to survive many of them.

The strongest friendships, in short, are not perfect; they are maintained. A few minutes of attention, repeated across years, will usually outlast a single extravagant gesture, because it is repetition that builds the expectation of being remembered. Friendship, on this view, is less a possession than a practice, and like any practice it rewards those who return to it regularly.

articles.title: The Insect Decline
articles.summary: 昆虫数量正在下降，影响授粉、食物链和生态系统。栖息地丧失、农药和气候变化是主要压力，保护昆虫也是保护人类。

Insects are easy to overlook. They are small, abundant, frequently unwelcome, and almost entirely absent from the way most people picture the natural world. Yet they pollinate a large share of the crops we eat, break down waste, feed birds and fish, and form the base of food chains that eventually include us. Their contribution is easily underestimated precisely because it is distributed across so many species and so much ordinary ground, none of which commands attention until it stops.

Surveys from several regions point in the same troubling direction: populations are falling. The causes are familiar, though their interaction is not. Loss of habitat as land is converted, intensive farming, pesticide use, pollution and a changing climate all exert pressure, and no single factor accounts for every decline; in any given place several may reinforce one another, which is precisely what makes the problem difficult to attribute and easy to postpone.

Some species are adapting, shifting their ranges or their timing, while others are quietly disappearing. Because insects are small and poorly recorded, the loss is hard to see, and a decline that leaves no visible trace can nonetheless be substantial. Absence, in ecology as in medicine, is often the hardest symptom to notice until it is advanced, and by then the condition may be far less reversible than it appears.

Protection, fortunately, does not require saving every species individually. It requires protecting habitats, reducing pesticide use where it is not necessary, and connecting green spaces so that populations are not stranded on isolated fragments. Gardens, parks, road verges and farmland can all contribute, and measures that help insects tend to help other wildlife as well. Insects are not a nuisance to be eliminated before the real business of living can proceed. They are part of the system that feeds us, and their absence would be far larger than they are.

articles.title: The Cheap-Housing Advantage

For decades, several American states attracted new residents chiefly by being cheap. A family could sell a modest home in an expensive coastal city and buy something considerably larger elsewhere, trading density and climate for space and disposable income. That advantage helped smaller cities grow, gave workers an alternative to the most costly metropolitan areas, and quietly subsidised the employers who located there, since a workforce that can afford to live nearby is a workforce that can be recruited.

Cheapness, however, is not self-sustaining. When demand rises faster than construction, prices follow, and the mechanism that once attracted people begins to repel them. Local rules restricting new housing, often defended by existing residents with entirely understandable motives, limit how quickly supply can respond. Investors who buy up stock reduce what remains available to families, and the cumulative effect is a market that is affordable in name while becoming unaffordable in practice. Affordability, it turns out, is a condition that must be reproduced year after year rather than a status once achieved.

Once the advantage erodes, the consequences extend well beyond individual household budgets. Employers find it harder to recruit, because a wage that looks generous in one region buys very little in another. Young people postpone moves, or abandon them altogether. Local services lose the residents whose taxes and labour sustain them, and housing quietly becomes an instrument of regional inequality, determining not merely where people live but which places are permitted to grow.

The policy question, then, is whether fast-growing regions will build enough homes to keep costs within reach. If they do, cheap housing can remain a durable foundation for growth; if they do not, it may prove a brief chapter rather than a lasting model. A region that cannot house its workers will struggle to keep its economy expanding, whatever its other advantages, and the shortage will be felt first by those with the least room to absorb it.

articles.title: The Last Quiet Place

In a world of traffic, aircraft and constant notification, silence has become one of the scarcest resources on the planet. Some of the quietest remaining places are now protected not only for the wildlife they contain but for their soundscapes, the whole audible texture of a landscape, which is as much a part of it as its trees and rivers. Sound, after all, is how a place announces that it is alive, and its disappearance is often the first sign that something has gone wrong.

Noise is a form of pollution, and its effects are more than aesthetic. It masks the calls of birds and whales, disrupts sleep and raises stress in humans who would not describe themselves as troubled by it. For many animals, sound is a matter of survival rather than ambience: it is how they find mates, warn of danger and locate food across distances they cannot see. When human noise saturates an environment, those signals are drowned out, and the species most dependent on hearing are often the least able to compensate. What looks like an empty forest may in fact be a conversation that has simply become inaudible to us.

Quiet places have scientific value as well. A recording of an intact soundscape supplies a baseline against which later change can be measured, and it can reveal species that are present but seldom seen, creatures whose existence is audible long before it is visible. More fundamentally, such recordings remind us that nature is not only a view. It is also a sound, and a landscape stripped of its sound is diminished in ways that a photograph cannot show.

Protecting quiet does not mean banning human activity from every wild place. It means managing noise, restricting the loudest uses, and treating places where natural sound persists as worth preserving in their own right. Silence, properly understood, is not empty. It is full of information, and once a soundscape is lost it is very difficult to restore.

articles.title: Higher Education's AI Problem
articles.summary: 大学既要利用 AI，又要保护学术诚信和学习质量。检测工具不可靠，课程设计、师生沟通和评价方式需要一起改变。
articles.text:
Universities are under pressure to respond to artificial intelligence, and the pressure arrives from several directions at once. Students use it to write, summarise and solve problems; faculty are divided between curiosity, alarm and simple exhaustion; administrators want clear rules, though the technology evolves faster than any committee can draft them. Where formal rules are absent, custom quietly fills the gap, and individual instructors end up making policy for their own courses because nobody else has made it for them.

Assessment is the most immediate difficulty. Take-home essays were already hard to verify, and AI makes them considerably harder; detection tools are imperfect, producing false accusations along with true ones, and damaging the trust they are supposed to protect. Some universities are therefore returning to in-class writing, oral examinations and process-based assignments that require drafts and reflection. These are more demanding to organise and harder to scale, but they reveal more about learning than a polished final product ever could.

A second difficulty is equity, and it receives less attention than it deserves. Students with access to better tools, faster connections and private tutoring may convert the same technology into a visible advantage, while others are penalised for using it in less polished ways, or for declining to use it at all. A policy focused exclusively on cheating will miss these deeper inequalities, and may even intensify them by punishing the students who have the least support behind them.

No single ban or product will resolve any of this. What is required is a coherent approach: clear expectations, genuine support for teachers, accessible guidance for students, and forms of assessment that value thinking rather than the appearance of fluency. The aim is not to defend the traditional essay as such, but to defend the learning that the essay was designed to reveal. That is slower and far less satisfying than a ban, yet it is the only response likely to hold once the next tool arrives.

articles.title: What Your Mouth Says About You
articles.summary: 口腔里的微生物与饮食、卫生和全身健康有关。刷牙、使用牙线、少吃糖，比追求“无菌”更重要。

The human mouth hosts several hundred species of bacteria, the great majority of which are harmless and a minority positively useful. Together they form what researchers call the oral microbiome: a dense community that colonises the teeth, the gums and the tongue. Because it is a community rather than a collection of isolated organisms, its internal balance — which species flourish and which are held in check — matters far more than the sheer number of microbes present. Diversity, in this context, is a mark of stability rather than of threat.

That balance is easily disturbed. Sugary food, for instance, nourishes acid-producing bacteria whose by-products erode tooth enamel, while inadequate brushing allows plaque, a sticky film of bacteria, to accumulate along the gum line and provoke inflammation. Frequent snacking is more damaging than a single sweet course, since it keeps the acid bath renewed and gives saliva too little time to neutralise it. What begins as a local irritation may not stay local: gum disease has been associated with conditions elsewhere in the body, including heart disease and diabetes, although the relationship is complex and unlikely to be simple.

It follows that oral care should aim not at sterility but at equilibrium. Brushing twice a day, cleaning between the teeth and limiting sugary snacks are unglamorous measures, yet they achieve more than any single product advertised as a quick solution. Drinking water and eating fibre-rich foods, which help to stimulate saliva and clear away food debris, offer modest additional support.

A healthy mouth, then, is something more than the cosmetic asset implied by a pleasant smile. It is an integral part of general health, and one of the few parts that can be influenced by ordinary daily conduct. Over the years the mouth accumulates not only plaque but habit; small practices, consistently repeated, count for more than occasional bursts of effort, and no mouthwash compensates for a week of neglect. The mouth, in this sense, is where private routine meets long-term health.

articles.title: Happiness Is Shared
articles.summary: 幸福不只来自收入或成就，也与人与人之间的联系有关。稳定的关系、面对面的相处和归属感，能显著影响生活满意度。

Ask what makes people happy and the answer will usually include money. Income does help, but it is not the whole answer: once basic needs have been satisfied, other goods begin to dominate — health, a sense of purpose, personal freedom and, above all, relationships. What the question tends to overlook is that happiness is rarely pursued directly; it arrives as a by-product of other commitments.

The pattern is consistent. People with close friends and family tend to report higher levels of well-being, and they cope better with stress and with illness; loneliness, by contrast, is associated with poorer mental and physical health. The mechanism is not mysterious: relationships supply practical help, emotional support and a sense of being needed, each of which shapes how a person weathers difficulty. Loneliness, in other words, is not simply the absence of company but the absence of people who would notice if something went wrong.

Connection, however, is not a matter of quantity. A handful of reliable relationships can be worth more than an extensive network of acquaintances, and the trust on which such relationships depend is built slowly, through face-to-face time, shared meals and ordinary conversation — the kind of contact that messages, for all their convenience, rarely reproduce. A large network, by contrast, may demand constant maintenance while offering little support at the moment it is needed.

None of this implies that people should be sociable at all times, since solitude has its own value and not everyone draws strength from company in the same measure. But humans are social animals, and a life in which there is nobody to call in a crisis is harder to sustain, however successful it may look from the outside. The conclusion is narrower: the capacity to form and sustain relationships is itself a skill, and one on which the value of other goods depends. Happiness, on this account, is less a private achievement than a shared condition; and a society that genuinely values connection ought to make time and space for it.

articles.title: The Classroom Backlash Against AI
articles.summary: AI 进入课堂后，一些学校开始反弹。过度依赖工具、检测不可靠和学术诚信问题，让师生重新讨论什么才是学习。
articles.text:
Artificial-intelligence tools entered classrooms accompanied by promises of efficiency. They could help students to brainstorm, to have a difficult concept explained in different words, and to receive feedback at any hour of the day. Many teachers were curious and not a few were enthusiastic. That early welcome, however, has given way in many places to a growing backlash.

Part of the concern is dependence. When a tool can produce an answer within seconds, students may be tempted to skip the very struggle — drafting, revising, getting something wrong — through which understanding is built. Teachers report work that looks polished but reads as shallow, competent in form and thin in substance. A child who has moved, talked and played returns to the desk more ready to sit still and think — an unnatural thing to ask of any young body for hour after hour. Play is not the opposite of learning. It is one of the principal ways in which children learn.

In higher education the stakes can feel high. That means feedback specific enough to be useful, opportunities to revise and resubmit, and a culture in which asking for help is unremarkable rather than shameful. It also means distinguishing, explicitly and repeatedly, between a mistake and a failure of worth: a bad essay is not evidence of a bad person, nor a low mark a permanent verdict on ability.

A university that rewards only flawless performance may produce graduates who are afraid to experiment, while one that teaches resilience may produce graduates who can adapt when the experiment fails — as, sooner or later, it will. articles.title: The Course in Failure

They read case studies of products that nobody wanted, companies that collapsed, scientific ideas that were pursued for years and then abandoned. The purpose is not to celebrate failure but to understand it — to examine, with the same rigour applied to success, the processes by which intelligent people arrive at conclusions that do not hold. The premise is that failure, properly examined, is a more instructive teacher than success, because success conceals the part played by luck.

Failure is rarely tidy. A project may fail for several reasons at once: bad timing, poor communication, insufficient resources, or an assumption that seemed reasonable at the outset and was never tested. Close examination of such cases reveals what success stories conceal, for the stories that survive tend to be told backwards, with the eventual outcome lending coherence to decisions that were, at the time, guesses. Survivorship bias — the habit of studying only the winners and ignoring the many attempts that came to nothing — distorts the lessons that can be drawn.

Students also learn about the emotional life of failure. It brings shame, and shame is a poor adviser: it discourages people from asking for help, from admitting uncertainty and from trying again. A classroom that treats failure as evidence to be examined, rather than as a verdict on the person who produced it, makes experiment safer and therefore more likely. Courses of this kind are less an invitation to fail than an attempt to lower the fear that makes failure unmentionable.

The lesson is not that failure is good. It is that failure is information, and the question is whether people are permitted to use it. An organisation, or a society, that punishes every mistake may become cautious, conformist and less capable of innovation, having trained its members to conceal the very evidence from which they might learn. Because rest is commonly imagined as a switch that flips once the day is over, people who cannot sleep try harder, retiring earlier, staying in bed longer, refining an ever more elaborate routine, only to discover that sleep withdraws the more insistently it is chased. The paradox is uncomfortable, since it turns a biological need into one more performance to be managed and scored.

Sleep specialists begin elsewhere: with a fixed hour of waking, kept even after a wretched night, for it is regularity that allows the body clock to settle. If sleep refuses to come, they advise rising to do something quiet rather than lying awake in bed, since a bed associated with frustration teaches the brain precisely the wrong association. Light matters equally: morning daylight anchors the internal clock, while bright screens late at night push it backwards. Caffeine, whose effects persist for hours, may still be active at midnight if drunk in the afternoon; alcohol is a subtler trap, for the drowsiness it brings is often followed by sleep that breaks later in the night. Each of these is a lever rather than a command, to be adjusted according to what the individual body tolerates.

None of this amounts to a quick fix. Sleep is simultaneously a skill and a biological process, and to treat it as a test of willpower is usually to prolong the very difficulty one hopes to overcome. What helps is not a single flawless night but small, consistent adjustments maintained long enough for the body to register the pattern; the aim, in effect, is to remove obstacles rather than to add effort. Improvement is gradual and rarely linear, which is why a poor night is better treated as information than as failure.

A good night, on this view, is not a performance to be assessed. It is a return to a rhythm the body already knows; hence consistency, rather than perfection, is the more useful ambition. Playing an instrument engages several systems at once. The player listens, reads or recalls notes, moves the fingers and monitors timing, all within a single act. Such coordination may strengthen connections among brain regions, and it draws heavily on attention and working memory, capacities on which almost every everyday task depends. Because the demands change as a piece is learned, practice keeps presenting the brain with problems it cannot solve automatically; nothing about this requires talent, only the willingness to remain a beginner.

What music provides, its advocates argue, is a structured and enjoyable way to practise something new, which is precisely what many adults stop doing once formal education ends.

Professional attainment is beside the point. A few minutes of practice, a simple instrument or a place in a community music group may be enough to begin, and the social side of making music together may matter as much as the notes. Progress is measured in months rather than days, which is itself a useful lesson for a culture accustomed to quick results. The aim is not mastery but engagement: to give the brain a fresh problem to solve and to keep curiosity alive.

The very efficiency that makes modern work possible is, in this respect, an obstacle to the relationships that make the work bearable.

The object is not to accumulate contacts but to create the conditions under which repeated, low-pressure time together becomes possible. Rewilding usually begins with a simple hope: restore a missing species and the ecosystem will mend itself. In Patagonia, the return of pumas has told a more complicated story, for the big cats have been observed hunting penguins, prey that few would expect a land predator to take. The image is striking, and it has been seized on by supporters and critics alike, each side reading it as confirmation of a different argument.

The discovery is not evidence that rewilding has failed. It demonstrates, rather, how thoroughly an ecosystem rearranges itself once a top predator reappears. Pumas may alter where penguins nest, how other predators behave and how nutrients circulate between land and sea; some of these effects will be welcome, while others may generate fresh conflicts with conservation goals. A predator's presence, moreover, can be felt by species it never touches, since vigilance itself consumes the time and energy that would otherwise go to feeding, breeding or simply resting.

Scientists accordingly remain cautious. A single observation is not a full picture, and long-term data on diet, population and behaviour are needed before anything can be said with confidence. Local communities, moreover, must be involved, since predators affect livestock as well as tourism, and a programme that ignores those costs is unlikely to endure. Conservation, in such places, is as much a matter of negotiation as of biology, and compensation schemes may buy time without buying trust.

The wider lesson is that nature does not revert to an earlier state the way a file is restored from a backup. Restoration creates a new set of relationships among species, people and place, which is why monitoring and flexibility matter quite as much as the initial release. The most surprising results, inconvenient as they are, tend to be the ones that teach us how little we know.

articles.title: Sleep Is a Skill
articles.summary: 睡眠不是关掉开关，而是受行为、环境和心理影响的技能。固定作息、减少卧床焦虑、管理光线和咖啡因，比追求完美睡眠更实际。

Sleep is often described as a switch that turns off at night. It is better understood as a process shaped by behaviour, environment and expectation, which explains why those who sleep well are not necessarily trying harder than the rest of us. They have built, often without noticing, the conditions that make sleep likely, and those conditions can be learned. Expectation is easily overlooked: a person convinced that eight uninterrupted hours are mandatory will read every waking moment as evidence of failure.

Regularity is one such condition. Going to bed and waking at roughly the same hour allows the body clock to anticipate rest, so that sleepiness arrives at the appointed time rather than at random. Another is the association between bed and sleep: if the bed becomes a place for scrolling, working or worrying, the brain learns an association that undermines the very purpose of lying down.

Light and caffeine exert a powerful influence as well. Morning light promotes alertness, whereas bright light at night delays sleep; caffeine can remain in the body for hours, and alcohol, though it may hasten the onset of sleep, tends to disturb it later. Timing matters as much as quantity: a late-afternoon coffee and an evening drink can both leave traces that the sleeping brain must work around. None of this demands a perfect routine, only small, consistent adjustments that are easier to sustain than a regime abandoned after a week.

The most unhelpful idea of all may be that sleep should be effortless. Trying to force it generates anxiety, and anxiety is precisely what keeps sleep at bay; the harder one watches the clock, the more remote the goal becomes. Far better to build the conditions and then let sleep arrive of its own accord. Sleep is not a test of willpower; it is a skill of letting go, and like most such skills it improves with practice rather than with pressure.

Strength deserves equal attention, though it is often neglected by people who equate fitness with endurance. articles.title: Why Your Brain Cannot Really Multitask
articles.summary: 同时处理多个任务时，大脑其实在不断切换。切换会消耗时间、增加错误，也会让人更难回到原来的专注状态。
articles.text:
Multitasking feels efficient. We answer a message, glance at a document and listen to a meeting, all within the same minute, and the impression of productivity is hard to resist. The brain, however, is not performing these actions simultaneously; it is switching rapidly between them, and every switch carries a cost that is rarely noticed at the time.

In one experiment, participants moved back and forth between two simple tasks. Those who switched frequently took longer to finish and made more mistakes than those who completed one task before starting the next. The difference was slight when measured over a minute, but it accumulated across a working day, which is why the habit can be so expensive while feeling so harmless. The finding has been repeated often enough that the pattern now looks less like a quirk of the laboratory than a feature of ordinary office life.

Switching also taxes attention. A quick look at a phone can pull the mind away from a difficult sentence, and returning to the same level of focus may take several minutes; this is why a brief interruption often feels far longer than it is. Even the anticipation of a message can divide attention before the message arrives. The residue of the abandoned task lingers, competing with the one supposedly resumed, and the resulting fog is easily mistaken for tiredness.

Some activities are simple enough to combine: listening to music while cleaning, for instance, imposes little conflict. Reading, writing and problem-solving, by contrast, demand sustained attention, and for these, doing one thing at a time is not old-fashioned reticence but a way of protecting the quality of thought. Batching similar tasks, silencing notifications and reserving a fixed hour for demanding work are modest remedies, yet they work because they reduce the number of switches rather than the effort spent on each.

In one small study, volunteers took a ten-minute walk after dinner. What matters is interrupting long stretches of sitting rather than achieving any particular speed or distance, so the habit can be attached to something already done every day.

Doctors are careful to add that walking is no substitute for medicine or a healthy diet, and for some patients it must be adapted to their condition. For many others, however, a brief walk after a meal is a low-risk habit with a plausible benefit, and small studies of this kind are a reminder that useful advice need not be complicated.
