articles.title: Why Some Streets Are Hotter Than Others
articles.summary: 同一座城市，不同街道夏天温度可能差很多。树木、浅色屋顶和透水地面能降温；缺少绿荫的社区往往更热。

On a hot summer day, two streets in the same city can feel entirely different. One is shaded and bearable; the other radiates heat like an oven. The difference is largely a matter of trees, and a growing number of cities have begun to treat them as essential infrastructure rather than as decoration.

Measurement comes first. A city cannot protect what it has never counted, so planners map street trees, record their size and species, and note where shade falls during the hottest hours. Such maps tend to confirm what residents already know: poorer districts have fewer trees and hotter streets. Trees, moreover, are unevenly distributed, and the districts with the least shade are often those whose residents can least afford to escape the heat. Because heat is invisible on ordinary maps, the exercise of counting is itself a political act, making visible an inequality that is otherwise felt only in summer.

Cities are responding with practical measures. Planting trees provides shade and cools the air through evaporation; painting roofs in light colours reflects sunlight; replacing concrete with gardens or permeable surfaces allows rainwater to soak into the ground and reduces the heat stored in the fabric of the street. Each intervention buys a little comfort, and together they can lower the temperature of a whole block. None of these measures is technically difficult, though each requires money and maintenance that cash-strapped districts rarely have in abundance.

These measures cost less than installing more air-conditioning, yet they demand patience and planning, for a young tree takes years to grow into shade and the benefits arrive long after the photographs are taken. Nor is planting a one-off act: young trees need watering, pruning and protection if they are to survive their first summers. The lesson is that shade is not a luxury. It is basic urban infrastructure, as necessary as roads and water pipes, and it should be planned with the same seriousness.

articles.title: Why Boredom Is Worth Keeping
articles.summary: 无聊不一定是坏事。放下手机、让思绪漫游，反而可能激发创造力和自我反思。
articles.text:
Few emotional states are dismissed as quickly as boredom, which we tend to treat as a defect to be remedied — usually by reaching for a phone. Yet boredom appears to serve a purpose. Deprived of a task to occupy it, the mind does not simply idle; it begins to wander, retrieving half-forgotten experiences and juxtaposing ideas that had no obvious connection. What looks from the outside like wasted time may be among the more productive things the brain does.

Psychologists who have let participants sit through tedious tasks before testing them report that such people often perform better on subsequent creative problems. The effect is not magic, nor is it a reason to inflict dullness on anyone. Boredom opens a space in which the brain goes looking for something worth attending to, and it is precisely the unpleasantness of that space — the mild itch of having nothing to do — that supplies the motive. Fill the space at once with short videos and the search never begins; the itch is scratched before it can direct attention anywhere.

Boredom also functions as a signal, telling us something about our own priorities. A meeting that strikes us as tedious may simply not concern anything we value; a weekend that feels hollow may reveal how long we have been too busy to notice what we have been missing. Such signals are uncomfortable, and the temptation is to silence them quickly, but they carry information that no amount of stimulation will supply.

None of this argues for seeking boredom all day, still less for romanticising it. The point is narrower: we might stop treating every quiet moment as a small failure to be corrected. A walk taken without headphones, a wait endured without a screen, a few minutes spent staring out of a window while nothing in particular happens — these are not gaps in an otherwise full life. They are, if we let them be, gifts we make to a mind that rarely gets to think without being prompted.

articles.title: The Paper Ceiling
articles.summary: 学历通胀让越来越多岗位要求大学文凭，即使工作内容没有改变。文凭成了筛选工具，却未必能证明岗位真正需要的能力。
articles.text:
A generation ago, a high-school diploma was sufficient for a great many office jobs. Today the same positions are frequently advertised with a degree requirement, although the work itself has changed remarkably little. Sociologists describe the resulting pattern as credentialism: the conviction that formal qualifications constitute the most reliable measure of a person's ability. The term is deliberately unflattering, and it captures something real — a habit of inferring competence from parchment rather than from evidence.

Screening explains part of the appeal. Faced with several hundred applications for a single post, an employer who filters by degree can reduce the pile in an afternoon, and the shortcut is hard to resist. Degrees are also read as signals — of persistence, of general intelligence, of a willingness to finish something tedious. The trouble is that the signal is coarse. It discriminates poorly among candidates, and it says almost nothing about creativity, about teamwork, or about the particular skills a job actually demands.

The costs of this convenience are borne largely by the young. Prolonged education means higher fees and a later entry into the workforce, and students from poorer families, for whom debt is not an abstraction, are understandably reluctant to take the gamble. Meanwhile the occupations that genuinely require training — the skilled trades prominent among them — struggle to recruit, since they carry less prestige than a desk job that asks for a degree nobody uses.

Some employers are therefore experimenting with skills-based hiring, setting candidates realistic tasks instead of screening them by certificate. Such methods can widen the talent pool, but they cost time and demand confidence in one's own judgement, which is precisely what the degree filter spared. Credentialism will not vanish overnight; it will recede only when employers stop treating a degree as a lazy shortcut and start specifying what a job actually requires. Online micro-credentials complicate the picture further. A short course can certify a specific competence without the expense of a full degree, and employers may well value the result — but the market is crowded, quality varies widely, and in the absence of clear standards learners can accumulate certificates that flatter a CV without improving their prospects.

articles.title: Free Buses and the Cost of Belonging

articles.text:
In a number of French cities the buses now run free of charge. The reasoning is disarmingly simple: if public transport costs the passenger nothing, more people will leave their cars at home, and the streets will be quieter, cleaner and safer. Supporters add a second argument, one that has less to do with traffic than with justice. Access to the city — to work, to appointments, to friends — should not be rationed by the price of a ticket, and those on low incomes are precisely the people for whom a fare, however modest, becomes a reason to stay at home.

The early evidence is mixed, though not discouraging. Ridership has risen, most sharply on short journeys and among the young and the elderly, and some drivers report that their buses now feel like a public service rather than a business with a timetable. Yet free fares are not a cure-all. Where buses are infrequent, or where the network stops short of the outskirts, households keep their cars regardless; a fare of zero does little for a passenger who cannot get where she needs to go.

The money, moreover, has to come from somewhere. Local taxes, national funding and the savings that follow from removing ticket machines and inspectors can cover part of the loss, but rarely all of it. Critics make an argument worth taking seriously: the same sum, spent on more frequent and more reliable services, might do more for passengers than the abolition of the fare. Reliability, after all, is what people plan their lives around.

The larger lesson is that transport policy is never only about price. It is about access, about time and — a word rarely heard in transport planning — about dignity. A free bus that comes once an hour is less useful than a cheap one that comes every ten minutes. Cities that have abolished fares are therefore asking, whether they say so or not, a deeper question: who should pay for the connections that make urban life possible? Where free fares have worked best, they have formed part of a wider programme — more frequent buses, better routes, stops that feel safe after dark. Without such changes, a free ticket risks being merely a cheaper way to wait.

articles.title: The Four-Day Week Comes to the Office
articles.summary: 四天工作制试验显示，减少工时不一定降低产出。企业通过缩短会议、增加专注时间维持效率，但医院、餐厅等行业难以照搬。
articles.text:
The four-day week has migrated from the management seminar to the payroll, and the results of the first large experiments are now coming in. In several countries firms have cut the working week to four days while holding pay constant, and many report that output has stayed level or edged upward — a finding that would have seemed implausible to an earlier generation of managers.

The explanation is not that employees cram five days of effort into four. In most trials they work fewer hours and waste less of them. Meetings are shortened or abolished, email is checked at intervals rather than continuously, and the working day is broken into longer stretches of uninterrupted concentration. In firms whose product is essentially thought, these adjustments can be sufficient to protect productivity; the hours removed were, in many cases, the least productive ones.

Advocates emphasise well-being, and here the evidence is more consistent. Workers report sleeping better, feeling less harried and spending more time with their families. Some employers add a commercial argument: staff are less likely to leave, and reduced turnover lowers the cost of hiring and training — an advantage that counts for a great deal in a tight labour market.

The picture darkens wherever output is tied to hours worked. A hospital, a restaurant or a factory cannot compress five days into four without hiring additional staff or shortening its opening hours, and for such employers the reform may raise costs rather than lower them. The debate, then, is not really about whether people want more free time — most plainly do — but about how work is organised, and whether firms are willing to redesign it rather than merely truncate it. The British and Japanese trials deserve to be read with care: participants volunteered, many worked in offices rather than on production lines, and the British pilot, though it involved dozens of companies and thousands of workers, was no random sample. Its results are encouraging but not universal, and its most transferable lesson may be the least dramatic — that fewer meetings and protected concentration improve work even when the week remains five days long.

articles.title: The Business of Holding Your Gaze
articles.summary: 注意力经济靠用户停留时间获利。平台用推荐和通知延长使用，但越来越多的人开始反感，并尝试用订阅、限时工具改变激励。
articles.text:
For years digital platforms have competed for a single scarce resource, and it has not been money. The longer a user stays, the more advertisements she is shown and the more behavioural data she surrenders; success has therefore been counted in minutes, clicks and daily active users. The model generated extraordinary profits and, in roughly equal measure, an extraordinary sense of exhaustion.

Users have grown steadily more vocal about feeds that seem engineered to prolong scrolling rather than to help them finish what they came for. Parents worry about their children, employees about their own concentration, and even some technology executives confess to restricting their own screen time. An industry that once presented itself as the emblem of innovation now finds its central business model the subject of public criticism — a reversal no product launch could have achieved.

Some companies have begun to experiment with different yardsticks. Rather than asking how long people remain, they ask whether users found what they needed and whether they would recommend the service to someone else. Others have built tools that help people impose limits on themselves: reminders to take a break, settings that suppress notifications after dark, daily time budgets that must be deliberately overridden. Such features are cheap to add and easy to advertise.

Sceptics reply that these gestures may amount to little more than marketing, since a platform can promote well-being in one panel of its app while profiting from compulsive use in another. Genuine reform, they argue, requires a different business model — subscription, most obviously, which does not depend on advertising. The distinction matters because advertising metrics reward time spent rather than value received: a user who opens an app to read a single message and remains for an hour counts as a triumph under the old regime. A subscription reverses the incentive, since the platform is paid whether the customer stays two minutes or two hours and can therefore afford to let her leave. That is a small shift in accounting and a considerable one in principle. The question is no longer merely how to capture attention but how to deserve it.

articles.title: The Water Beneath Our Feet
articles.summary: 地下水看不见，却支撑农业和饮水。过度抽取会导致地面下沉、海水入侵；需要测量、定价和跨区域合作。
articles.text:
Ask anyone to picture fresh water and the image that comes back is almost always a river or a lake. In reality a large share of the world's fresh water lies underground, held in the pores of rock and the spaces between soil particles, and it is this hidden reserve that supplies farms, factories and millions of homes. Because it cannot be seen, it is easy to forget — until a well runs dry.

Groundwater is not, however, unlimited, and its rates of renewal are geologically slow: an aquifer may take decades or centuries to refill. Pump it faster than it is replenished and the consequences surface, literally. The land above may subside as the supporting water is withdrawn, cracking foundations and permanently reducing the capacity of the aquifer. Along coasts there is a second danger, since seawater can intrude into the emptied spaces and render what remains too salty to drink or to spread on crops.

The problem is sharpest where agriculture depends on irrigation. In a dry year a farmer has little practical choice but to pump more, and in the absence of agreed rules each user has an incentive to extract as much as possible before a neighbour does — a logic that reliably produces the outcome nobody wants.

Solutions are difficult but not impossible, and they begin with measurement: what can be counted can be argued about. Realistic pricing encourages efficiency, while compensation for farmers can make conservation financially survivable rather than merely virtuous. Because aquifers ignore administrative boundaries, agreements across regions are indispensable, and the necessary first step is to treat groundwater as a shared resource rather than a private well. California supplies a cautionary case. During a severe drought, farmers pumped so heavily that some wells failed and the land sank by several metres; the state eventually required local agencies to manage groundwater sustainably, but implementation has been slow. The episode suggests a general pattern: regulation tends to arrive after the damage has become visible, and farmers need support if they are to adapt in time.

articles.title: When a Degree Becomes the Minimum
articles.summary: 学历要求不断升高，部分原因是筛选方便，而非岗位真的需要。学历通胀让年轻人投入更多，却未必获得相应回报。
articles.text:
The minimum has moved. Where a high-school diploma once opened the door to a wide range of office work, the same posts now routinely carry a degree requirement, though the duties attached to them have scarcely altered. Economists call the result credential inflation: the qualification demanded for a given job rises while the job itself stays where it was. Inflation is the right metaphor, because what has grown is not the skill the work requires but the paper certifying it.

Two forces sustain the spiral. The first is administrative convenience. When hundreds of people apply for one vacancy, a degree requirement separates them cheaply, and no hiring manager is criticised for insisting on it. The second is the faith that a degree encodes persistence and general ability — true on average, misleading in individual cases. A certificate says little about whether a candidate can hold a team together, improvise under pressure, or acquire the specific skills the post demands.

The bill is presented to the young. Longer study means higher fees, delayed earnings and, for students from poorer families, a debt that may not look like a reasonable bet. Nor is the distortion confined to universities. Occupations that genuinely need training — plumbing, electrical work, carpentry — struggle to recruit, because a culture that ranks degrees above apprenticeships has taught school-leavers to regard such work as second best.

Skills-based hiring is the most promising response available. Some employers now set candidates realistic tasks instead of sorting them by certificate; the approach broadens the field and can uncover talent the paper filter discarded, but it is slower and demands that managers trust their own judgement — exactly what the old shortcut spared them. Credential inflation will not be reversed by exhortation. It will ease only when employers stop using degrees as a lazy proxy and specify what a job actually requires. Online micro-credentials add a further twist: a short course can certify a narrow competence — data analysis, project management — without the cost of a degree, and employers may genuinely value it. But the market is crowded, quality varies enormously, and without clear standards learners can accumulate certificates that decorate a CV without improving their prospects, leaving the screening problem precisely where it was.

A fall in the number of applicants

articles.title: Start Before You Feel Ready
articles.summary: 拖延往往不是为了偷懒，而是为了逃避任务带来的不舒服。把任务拆到极小、先做两分钟，比等待“有状态”更容易开始。
articles.text:
Almost everyone procrastinates. We postpone a report, a reading assignment, an awkward email, fully aware that the delay will make us feel worse rather than better, and we do it anyway. The usual diagnosis — laziness — explains very little. What actually stops us is a feeling the task provokes and we would rather not have: boredom, or the fear of doing it badly, or the vaguer dread of discovering that we cannot do it at all. The avoidance is not irrational so much as short-sighted, a bargain that trades a moment's relief for a day's unease.

The most practical remedy is to shrink the first step until it no longer looks threatening. Not "write the essay" but "open the document and write one sentence"; not "study for two hours" but "read one page". A start of two minutes is almost impossible to refuse, and beginning, once it has happened, tends to change how the task feels. The dread belongs largely to the anticipation rather than to the work.

A second technique is to notice the excuse without obeying it. "I will do it when I feel ready" sounds like prudence and functions as postponement; readiness, in most people's experience, arrives after the beginning rather than before it. Recognising the sentence for what it is — a familiar piece of self-persuasion rather than a description of the future — deprives it of much of its authority.

Finally, it helps to be fair to yourself. Harsh self-criticism makes an already unpleasant task feel more threatening, and a mind that feels threatened responds by avoiding the threat. Self-compassion is not indulgence, still less permission to give up; it lowers the cost of returning after a lapse, which is the only thing that determines whether progress continues. Anything worth finishing is built out of small starts, repeated.

articles.title: The Manager Who Listens
articles.summary: 好的管理者不一定话最多。多听、少打断、允许沉默，能让团队更愿意报告问题，也更容易用上集体专业知识。
articles.text:
Meetings have a familiar shape: the manager speaks first and speaks longest. The pattern has the appearance of efficiency — whoever holds authority sets the direction, and everyone else responds to it. Research on how teams actually perform, however, points the other way. The managers whose teams learn fastest are often those who talk least, not because they have nothing to say but because they have arranged the conversation so that other people's knowledge can reach the surface.

Listening, in this sense, is not the same as waiting for a turn to speak. It means asking questions that cannot be answered in one word, tolerating silences long enough for someone else to fill them, and making disagreement cheap. The real test is what happens to bad news. A manager who greets it with blame teaches the team a durable lesson — that problems are safer unreported — and the next problem will be discovered later, by a customer. A manager who responds with curiosity hears about it while it is still small.

Quiet managers also leave room for expertise they do not possess. Any team is likely to contain people who understand the technology, the customers or the local conditions better than the person chairing the meeting. If the manager fills every pause, that knowledge stays where it is; if the manager leaves the pause open, it tends to emerge. A simple diagnostic is to count how often the manager speaks during the first ten minutes. If the answer is almost always, the team is probably holding something back.

This is not an argument for passivity. Managers must still set goals, make decisions and answer for both; a leader who listens and then does nothing has merely been agreeable. What matters is the order of operations — listen first, decide second, explain third — and the recognition that a pause after a question, awkward as it feels, frequently produces the most honest answer on offer. Listening, moreover, is a skill rather than a personality trait; it improves with practice, with feedback and with a genuine willingness to be surprised by what a team knows. A manager who says less can end up leading a team that thinks more, and small acts of attention, repeated, can reshape a department's habits.

articles.title: Who Pays for the News?
articles.summary: 广告收入下降后，新闻业转向订阅、公共资金和会员制。地方新闻的衰落尤其危险，因为民主需要关于社区的可靠信息。
articles.text:
For most of the twentieth century the economics of newspapers rested on a straightforward bargain. Readers paid a small sum for the paper; advertisers paid a much larger one for the attention that came with it. Journalism was, in effect, subsidised by commerce, and the subsidy was generous enough to support foreign bureaus, investigative teams and, in many towns, more than one daily.

The internet dissolved that bargain. Classified advertising — once the quiet engine of newspaper profits — migrated to specialist platforms that did the job better and cheaper, while social media captured the audience papers had assumed was theirs by habit. Newsrooms responded as any business would: they cut staff and closed bureaus. Some erected paywalls and asked readers to subscribe. For large titles with loyal readerships this can work, but it produces a division that ought to trouble anyone who cares about public information — between those who can afford reliable news and those who cannot.

Public funding is the obvious alternative, and it has a respectable record. Subsidy can sustain reporting that the market systematically undervalues: local courts, planning decisions, the slow investigative work that yields no immediate audience. Yet it raises an awkward question about independence. A newsroom that depends on politicians for its budget may hesitate to criticise them, and the hesitation need not be conscious to be real.

The decline that matters most is local. When a town loses its newspaper, fewer people turn up at public meetings and fewer officials are held to account; national politics receives more coverage than ever, but democracy also runs on information about the street, the school and the council. Non-profit newsrooms and public broadcasters are experimenting with memberships, foundations and endowments, though none is a complete answer. Membership builds a committed audience but may not reach enough of one; a foundation can protect independence while quietly shaping priorities. The search for a sustainable model is therefore also a search for a way to finance public-interest journalism without delivering it to the wealthy or to the state. How citizens learn what is happening around them remains, in the end, a political question disguised as a business one.

articles.title: Why Writing by Hand Still Matters
articles.summary: 手写比打字慢，但正因为慢，大脑有更多时间组织信息。手写笔记、草稿和思考，仍然是学习的重要工具。
articles.text:
In classrooms where laptops have largely displaced notebooks, the case for the pen can sound like nostalgia. Typing is faster, produces neater pages and leaves a searchable record. Yet handwriting has survived every prediction of its disappearance, and a considerable body of research suggests that removing it from the classroom would cost learners something that speed cannot repay.

Much of the explanation lies in what the hand cannot do. Because a writer by hand cannot transcribe every word, he or she must listen, select and compress — a slower operation that compels the brain to organise material rather than merely copy it. Hence the counter-intuitive finding, reported in several studies of university students, that those who take handwritten notes remember more of what they heard, even though their notes are shorter and less complete. Nor is the advantage confined to memory. Forming letters helps young children link sounds to shapes, an asset in early reading and spelling, while for older students the very slowness of writing out a plan or a difficult sentence can create the pause in which errors become visible and a half-formed idea is forced to declare itself.

None of this is an argument against keyboards. Typing serves long essays, editing and collaboration well, and a laptop can store what a pen cannot; a student revising from a searchable document is not being sentimental. What follows is not a hierarchy of tools but a division of labour: the machine for volume and revision, the hand for thought. Handwriting also leaves a personal trace — a correction, an arrow, a question pencilled in the margin — and that visible record lets a learner reconstruct how an idea developed rather than merely inspect the form in which it was finally submitted.

To defend handwriting, then, is not to reject the digital age but to insist that attention has more than one instrument. A pen is not a relic of a pre-digital past; it is a slower, and for some purposes more deliberate, way of paying attention.

articles.title: The Cost of Missing Sleep
articles.summary: 长期缺觉不只让人困，还会影响情绪、免疫力和判断力。固定作息、减少睡前屏幕，比周末补觉更有效。
articles.text:
Sleep is the resource people most readily borrow against, as though the hours could be repaid later at no interest. Students stay up to revise, employees answer email long after dinner, and almost everyone has watched one more video than intended. The bill, however, is not confined to the fatigue of the following morning, and it is presented to the body rather than to the calendar.

A large body of research associates poor sleep with disturbances of mood, attention and memory. Those who sleep badly tend to find their emotions harder to govern, and they appear more susceptible to ordinary infections such as colds. The comparison that public health campaigns keep returning to is driving: a motorist who has slept very little may be as impaired as one who has been drinking, though the sleepy driver is unlikely to be stopped, tested or ashamed.

The commonest remedy is also the least effective. Sleeping late at the weekend brings some relief, yet it does not undo the accumulated deficit of five short nights; the body does not settle its accounts so simply, and a pattern of late nights and late mornings can leave the internal clock further out of step than before. What helps more is regularity — retiring and rising at roughly the same hour — together with a calm prelude to the night: dimmed lights, the phone left in another room, a fixed bedtime. Small adjustments accumulate. Less caffeine after midday, a dark and quiet room, a consistent hour: none of these requires equipment or expense, and together they can improve sleep materially.

Sleep, after all, is neither a luxury nor a sign of laziness but part of the mechanism by which the body and the brain repair themselves. Protecting it is one of the more practical forms of preventive medicine, cheaper if not easier than treating what its absence produces. Persistent insomnia, however, is not a test of willpower; if poor sleep lasts for weeks, a doctor is a more sensible destination than another attempt to try harder.

articles.title: AI at Work: Replacement or Redesign?
articles.summary: AI 更容易替代任务，而不是整个职业。真正的问题是工作如何重新设计：哪些交给机器，哪些保留人的判断和关系。
articles.text:
Every general-purpose technology arrives accompanied by a fear of replacement, and artificial intelligence has proved no exception. It writes, summarises, translates and answers questions at a speed no clerk can match, and workers in customer service, administration and even law have reasonable grounds for anxiety. The forecasts offered to them alternate between reassurance and alarm, and neither is much help to someone whose daily work is being redesigned while the argument continues.

The picture, however, is more complicated than the headlines imply, because automation attaches itself to tasks rather than to whole occupations. A lawyer may spend fewer hours reviewing documents and more advising clients; a nurse may be released from paperwork only to spend longer at the bedside. What changes is the bundle of tasks that constitutes a job, and with it the skills that carry value. Prediction, in this light, is less a matter of counting jobs than of tracing which fragments of them can be handed to a machine.

Whether that change is welcome is not automatic. Where firms use AI chiefly to reduce headcount, the gains accrue to shareholders while the risk is borne by employees; where the same technology absorbs repetitive work, staff may recover time for judgement, creativity and relationships with clients. Policy is decisive as well: training, social protection and clear rules on data and accountability largely determine whether AI widens opportunity or deepens inequality. None of these outcomes is dictated by the software itself, which is why arguments that treat technology as a force of nature miss the point.

The danger, in short, is not that machines will abruptly do everything, but that the gains will be captured by a handful of firms while many workers lose bargaining power. Moving people into new tasks demands investment in training, not optimistic speeches about the future. For an individual, the more useful question is therefore not whether a machine will take the job, but which parts of it will change, and what can be learned next.

articles.title: The Ageing Century
articles.summary: 全球人口正在变老。老龄化不只是养老金压力，也意味着住房、医疗、交通和社区需要重新设计，以支持更长的生命。
articles.text:
Societies are growing older. Longer lives and smaller families mean that the number of people aged 60 or over is expected to double by 2050 — arguably the most consequential social change of the century, and one that will touch almost every institution, from the labour market to the design of a bus shelter.

Public discussion usually frames ageing as a financial question: who will pay for pensions and health care? The question is real, yet it is not the whole story, and treating it as the only story has consequences of its own. Older people contribute as workers, carers, volunteers and grandparents, and many remain active for decades after retirement. The task is to design systems that support that contribution rather than to treat its authors as a burden to be managed.

Housing offers one illustration. A city planned around young commuters can isolate residents who no longer drive, whereas better public transport, benches, accessible pavements and mixed neighbourhoods make an enormous difference to daily life. Health systems, similarly, must attend to long-term conditions rather than only to emergencies. Language matters too: describing older people solely as dependent can become a self-fulfilling description, and many want to work, learn and contribute if given flexible arrangements, accessible places and a measure of respect that does not condescend.

Ageing, then, is not a crisis to be resolved by a single policy but a long transition running through work, family, housing and health. Societies that plan early may turn longer lives into an achievement; those that wait will find the costs harder to manage. articles.title: A Walk in the Woods

Exercise has moved indoors. Gyms are convenient, the weather cannot spoil a session, and the machines measure everything from heart rate to pace. Yet a walk in a park or a wood may offer something a treadmill cannot: a change in the quality of attention.

Research on nature and mental health suggests that time outdoors lowers stress and lifts mood, and one explanation is that natural scenes make no demands. A tree, a path, a bird — none of them asks to be answered, decided upon or performed for. The mind rests, but differently from the way it rests indoors, where walls, screens and other people continue to solicit it. Writers on attention have long noticed that a landscape holds the eye without capturing it; what the outdoor setting removes is not stimulation but obligation.

Walking has physical benefits as well. It raises the heart rate gently, interrupts long stretches of sitting, and requires neither special clothing nor a membership; for those who find gyms intimidating, and they are more numerous than the industry likes to admit, a local park is the easiest of beginnings. Unlike a membership card, a footpath also survives the weeks when motivation is low, which is when most exercise programmes quietly end.

The effect should not be oversold. A walk is not a treatment for serious mental illness, and presenting it as one would be both dishonest and unkind to those who need clinical care. What a regular short walk can do is more modest and more durable: it gives a day a shape, gives the mind a little room, and belongs among the ordinary habits that sustain health rather than among the remedies that reverse disease. The appeal lies precisely in its modesty — no equipment, no audience, no fee. Sometimes the most reliable medicine is not a tablet but a path.

articles.title: The Joy of Missing Out

Much phone-checking is driven by anxiety rather than curiosity: a friend has posted a photograph, a group chat is moving quickly, a news story has broken. The feeling has a name — FOMO, the fear of missing out — and it has grown common enough to organise whole evenings, or to make a conversation with the person opposite feel like a pause between notifications.

Constant checking, however, is not free. It interrupts conversation, delays sleep and fragments work; more insidiously, it encourages the impression that other people's lives are more interesting than one's own, since what one sees is the edited version that others have chosen to publish. The result is a peculiar loneliness, in which a person is connected to everyone and present with no one. Nothing has been missed, and nothing has been enjoyed.

Against this, some have proposed JOMO, the joy of missing out. Its adherents switch off notifications, leave group chats, and spend an evening without a screen. The first hour is uncomfortable — the hand reaches for the phone unbidden, and the silence feels like a fault in the equipment — and then something unexpected happens: the world does not end, and the messages wait. Missing out, they discover, is not the same as being left out; it can be a decision, and by deciding what not to follow one makes room for what is actually valued: a conversation, a book, a walk, an hour of quiet.

The point is not to reject technology but to choose when to be available and when to be present, a distinction the devices themselves are designed to blur. A quiet evening may prove more memorable than a hundred updates, and unlike the updates it does not need to be reported to anyone. What begins as an experiment in unplugging usually settles into a smaller adjustment of habit rather than a conversion.

articles.title: Loneliness as a Health Issue

Loneliness is generally treated as a private sorrow, a matter for the individual and perhaps for a few friends. It is increasingly described, more accurately, as a public health issue. Those who feel isolated appear to run a higher risk of heart disease, depression and early death, and the mechanism is not merely mood: social connection seems to shape the way the body responds to stress, so that the absence of company registers physically rather than only emotionally. It is also a cost that health services, not merely families, end up paying.

Causes are multiple and often cumulative. Living alone, moving to a new city, losing a job or caring for a relative can each thin the ties that hold a life together, and they frequently arrive together. Retirement, too, can dissolve the daily collegiality on which many people had quietly depended. Young people are not exempt, even when they are permanently online. Digital contact may help, but it does not reliably replace the comfort of a physical presence — the difference between a message and someone in the room.

What works is rarely a single programme. Safe public spaces, affordable housing, accessible transport, employers who allow time for relationships, and community groups all contribute; so do small acts that cost almost nothing, such as a neighbour saying hello, a colleague inviting someone to lunch, or a doctor asking about social contact and waiting for the answer rather than moving on to the next item.

The lesson is that connection is infrastructure, not luxury. Treating loneliness purely as an individual failing puts the burden on those already struggling and misdescribes the problem, for connection is a condition that public choices can support or undermine. Doctors and employers can help by asking simple questions and making time for the answers, but the strongest protection is a society in which it is easier to meet, to belong, and to ask for help without shame.

articles.title: Art in the Open

Public art is easy to ignore. A statue in a square, a mural on a gable, a painted bench: after a few weeks it dissolves into the background, and residents pass it as they pass a lamp post. Yet such work can shape how people feel about a place, marking a neighbourhood's history, commemorating a local figure, or simply giving strangers a reason to stop and talk.

What distinguishes it from art in a museum is ownership. Public art belongs to everyone, which is both its strength and its difficulty: a work that one group finds meaningful may strike another as irrelevant or offensive, and neither group has the option of walking past the ticket desk. A monument that has offended nobody has, in all likelihood, said nothing. Controversy, unpleasant as it is, is not always a failure; it can indicate that a community is arguing about what it values, which is a form of civic health rather than a symptom of decline.

The more successful projects tend to involve local people from the outset. Artists listen to residents, learn the area's history and revise their plans accordingly; the result may be less polished than a work chosen by experts in an office, but it is far more likely to be cared for, defended and repaired. The process also leaves residents better able to say what they want from the place, which outlasts the object itself.

None of this makes public art a solution to urban problems. It cannot substitute for housing, schools or green space, and to pretend otherwise would be to mistake a pleasant surface for a policy. It can, however, remind people that a city is more than buildings — that it is a shared place with a shared story, and its defenders do best when they make the modest claim rather than the grand one.

articles.title: Learning Together, or Just Sitting Together?

articles.text:
Group work is now standard in schools and universities, defended on the grounds that it prepares students for workplaces where cooperation is unavoidable. The defence is reasonable, and it is also convenient, since group work lets one teacher supervise more students than individual tutorials would. Anyone who has completed a group project will recognise the risks: one student does most of the work, others vanish, and everyone receives the same grade.

Research on cooperative learning suggests that the method works, but only when it is structured. Students need a clear task, individual roles within it, and a reason to explain their thinking to one another. Divide the work and staple the pieces together, and they may learn less than they would have learned alone — less, because the parts never have to be reconciled, and the understanding that reconciliation produces is precisely the point.

A useful technique is to require each student to explain a part of the solution to the group, which makes individual understanding visible and gives quieter students a turn. Silence, in an unstructured group, is rarely neutrality. The teacher's role shifts accordingly: to set the rules, observe the process rather than the product, and intervene when one voice begins to dominate. None of this is easy to sustain, since explaining takes longer than dividing and the temptation to fall back on the simpler arrangement is considerable.

Group work, then, is a tool rather than a magic solution. Well designed, it teaches cooperation, communication and the value of another person's perspective; badly designed, it teaches students to avoid responsibility and to resent the grade they receive. The difference lies almost entirely in the design, and in the willingness of teachers to defend that design when the timetable tightens. A group that has been badly run teaches the opposite lesson, and teaches it thoroughly.

articles.title: The Habit Loop

articles.text:
Habits are actions repeated with so little deliberation that they seem to happen to us: brushing teeth, checking a phone, taking the same route to work. Psychologists describe them with a simple loop — a cue, a routine and a reward — a model that is useful precisely because it is unglamorous.

The cue is whatever starts the behaviour, a time of day or a passing feeling; the routine is the action itself; the reward is what the brain takes from it, whether relief, pleasure or a sense of completion. Repeated often enough, the loop strengthens until the behaviour feels normal, which is precisely what makes it hard to notice and harder to question. By the time a habit is established, the reward no longer needs to be large; the anticipation of it is sufficient.

This explains why willpower is a weak strategy. When cues are everywhere, resistance is exhausting and eventually fails, and each failure appears to confirm a personal weakness that the arrangement of the environment had already made likely. It is easier to change the environment: the phone left in another room, healthy food prepared in advance, running clothes laid out the night before. Such arrangements do not demand heroism; they make the desired action the path of least resistance. What looks like a failure of character is often a badly arranged room.

Small steps matter for the same reason. Someone who wants to read more might begin with a single page a night — a target so modest that it survives a bad day. The aim is not perfection but repetition: a behaviour easy enough to perform again tomorrow, and again the day after, each repetition making the next one marginally cheaper. Habits grow through repetition, not through a single dramatic decision, and the person who waits for motivation to arrive will usually wait a long time.

articles.title: Take the Meeting Outside

That most meetings unfold around a table, with participants seated, screens open and attention quietly drifting, is a convention so familiar that it is seldom examined. The walking meeting proposes an alternative: two or three colleagues conversing as they move through a park, along a corridor or down a quiet street. What begins as a change of venue, its advocates argue, soon becomes a change of atmosphere, because removing the table also removes the ritual of hierarchy arranged around it.

Those who favour the practice claim that its benefits are more than physical. Walking side by side, they observe, feels markedly less formal than sitting opposite someone, and the absence of a direct gaze appears to loosen the pressure to perform. For quieter members of a team this can be liberating: freed from the need to interrupt, they may say what they would otherwise have kept to themselves. Movement, meanwhile, is said to help ideas flow, and even a short walk interrupts the long stretches of sitting that office life imposes. Whether such effects can be measured, or whether they rest on the enthusiasm of converts, remains an open question, but the accounts of those who have tried it are consistent enough to deserve attention.

Yet the format has practical limits, and ignoring them would be naive. Walking meetings work best for conversation, planning and one-to-one discussion; they are far less suitable for detailed reports, large groups, or anyone obliged to take notes. Weather, accessibility and safety all matter, since not everyone can walk easily, and not every neighbourhood is pleasant enough for a productive exchange. A session that demands concentration, or a participant who tires after ten minutes, will expose the weaknesses of the arrangement at once.

The point, then, is not to replace every meeting but to match the setting to the task. A difficult conversation may require privacy and a table, whereas a creative discussion may benefit from fresh air and movement. Good work depends not only on what is discussed but also, as the advocates of walking remind us, on where.

articles.title: What Inflation Really Means
articles.summary: 通胀不是所有价格同时上涨，而是整体生活成本持续上升。它影响工资、储蓄和利率，也受预期影响。
articles.text:
To describe inflation simply as "prices going up" is close to the truth but not precise enough for serious use. The prices of individual goods rise and fall constantly, and a single expensive item tells us very little. Inflation, properly understood, is a sustained rise in the general level of prices across an economy. Statisticians estimate it by tracking a basket of goods and services that households typically buy, among them food, housing, transport and leisure; when the total cost of that basket rises over time, inflation is positive, and the rate matters because it measures how quickly money is losing its purchasing power. The composition of the basket is itself a matter of judgement, since what counts as typical spending shifts as habits do.

The effects are distributed unevenly. Someone with savings may find that cash buys less than it once did, while a worker whose wages fail to keep pace feels worse off with every month that passes. Borrowers, by contrast, may gain, since inflation erodes the real value of their debt, a gain that lenders absorb as a loss. It is largely for this reason that central banks, seeking to cool demand and bring prices under control, often raise interest rates.

Expectations complicate the picture further. Where people believe that prices will keep rising, they may demand higher wages or bring purchases forward, behaviour that can entrench the very inflation they fear and make it harder to control. Central banks therefore watch not only actual prices but also what households and businesses expect to happen next.

For ordinary households, the practical question is less the headline rate than their own basket: a student, a pensioner and a family with young children buy quite different things, and a single average can hide the fact that some people feel inflation far more sharply than others. Understanding this is a form of civic knowledge, helping people judge wage offers, savings and public promises.

articles.title: The Food We Throw Away
articles.summary: 全球大量食物在收获、销售和家庭中被浪费。减少浪费不仅节省金钱，也能减少水、土地和温室气体压力。

Every year a substantial share of the world's food is wasted. Some is lost on farms before it ever reaches a market, some spoils on shop shelves, and some is thrown away in ordinary kitchens. The waste is not merely a moral embarrassment; it also consumes water, land, energy and labour that might have been devoted to something else. Nor is the harm confined to those inputs, for food left to rot in landfill releases methane, so that waste quietly contributes to the climate problem with which it is seldom associated.

Households are among the largest sources. People buy more than they need, forget what is lurking at the back of the fridge, or cook far more than anyone intends to eat. Labels compound the confusion, since a "best before" date is usually a statement about quality rather than safety; food that looks and smells perfectly fine is nevertheless discarded because a number has passed. Redistribution schemes, food banks among them, rescue some of what would otherwise be lost, though they treat a symptom rather than its cause.

The responses available are, encouragingly, neither exotic nor expensive. Planning meals in advance, shopping from a list and storing food properly can cut waste substantially. Shops can offer smaller portions and clearer labelling, while cities can separate food waste and convert it into compost or energy rather than burying it. Households, for their part, can learn to read a date label with a degree of scepticism.

No single measure will solve a problem of this scale, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Yet wasting less food remains one of the most practical ways of reducing environmental pressure, and it begins with the fridge, the shop and the farm rather than with a government promise. Framed in that way, the issue is not about guilt at all; it is about designing a system that values what has already been grown, caught and transported.

articles.title: The Pressure on Young Minds
articles.summary: 青少年心理健康问题常被忽视。学业压力、家庭冲突、网络欺凌和缺乏支持都可能加重问题，倾听和及时求助很重要。
articles.text:
Adolescence is a period of rapid, sometimes bewildering change. Young people are forming an identity, building friendships and facing pressure at school, and for many this is an exciting time of discovery. For a substantial minority, however, it is overwhelming, and the signs are easily overlooked.

Mental health problems frequently begin in the teenage years. Anxiety, depression and eating disorders can disrupt sleep, concentration and relationships, and their effects ripple outward into family life and schoolwork. Some young people withdraw into silence; others become angry or reckless. Adults, seeing only the behaviour, may mistake these signs for laziness or simple bad conduct, so that the underlying distress goes unaddressed.

Several factors can contribute, often in combination: academic pressure, conflict at home, bullying, the relentless comparison that social media encourages, and a shortage of safe places in which to talk. What appears to protect young people is not any single intervention but the experience of being heard. Those who feel that an adult takes them seriously, and who know where to go for help, are considerably more likely to seek it. Stigma remains the largest obstacle of all, since a teenager who fears being labelled may conceal distress even from those closest to them, while the services that do exist are often underfunded or offered only after a long wait.

Schools and families need not solve every problem themselves, and expecting them to do so is unrealistic. They can, however, listen without judging, take warning signs seriously and connect young people with professional support. Asking "Are you okay?" is not a cure, but it can be a first step. Support works best when it is ordinary and ongoing rather than a crisis response: a trusted adult, a predictable routine and a safe place to speak can make a real difference to a young person who otherwise has none.

articles.title: Mental Health at Work
articles.summary: 工作环境会直接影响心理健康。压力、歧视、过长工时和缺乏支持会增加风险；合理分工、尊重和可获得的帮助能起到保护作用。
articles.text:
Work is far more than a source of income. It shapes identity, supplies social contact and imposes the routine around which the rest of life is organised. When work is well designed, it can sustain mental health; when it is not, it can steadily erode it.

The risks are familiar but often underestimated. Excessive workload, long hours, unclear expectations, discrimination and bullying all take a toll, and workers may feel unsafe asking for help, particularly when they fear losing their job. Remote work, for all its flexibility, can deepen isolation, while insecure contracts make even modest planning impossible. Stigma compounds the damage, since a culture that equates distress with weakness discourages precisely the early conversation that would help.

Responsibility is therefore shared. Employers clearly have a part to play, though governments and communities bear responsibility too. Good practice includes realistic workloads, clearly defined roles, training for managers and access to confidential support. Above all, it means treating mental health as part of health and safety rather than as a private weakness to be concealed until it becomes a crisis.

The cost of ignoring the problem is high, and it is ultimately paid by someone. Poor mental health reduces productivity, increases turnover and pushes people out of work altogether, whereas a workplace that protects mental health is not a luxury but a basic condition for sustainable work. Managers need not become therapists; they need to notice changes, ask privately and know where to refer someone, for small conversations can prevent long absences. A healthy workplace also permits recovery: those returning after illness require adjustments, not suspicion, and flexibility, clear communication and reasonable deadlines help them stay in work. Smaller employers often lack the resources to do this well, which is why external support and clear legal expectations matter. The cheapest intervention, though, is often the most human, which is simply to ask how someone is and to mean it.

articles.title: 251 Million Children Out of School
articles.summary: 尽管教育普及取得进展，仍有大量儿童和青少年失学。贫困、冲突、性别和地区差距是主要原因，仅建学校并不够。
articles.text:
The world has made genuine progress in education. More children attend primary school than a generation ago and literacy rates have risen, yet a UNESCO report estimates that 251 million children and young people remain out of school. The figure is a reminder that access to learning is still distributed very unequally.

Poverty is one cause. Families may depend on children's earnings, or may simply be unable to afford books, uniforms and transport. Conflict and displacement destroy schools and make the journey to them dangerous. Girls face additional barriers that boys do not, among them early marriage, unsafe routes and the expectation that they will assume care work at home.

The quality of schooling matters as much as access to it. A child who sits in an overcrowded class without trained teachers or adequate materials may learn very little, however regularly they attend. Distance is another obstacle, for a school that exists may still be hours away and unsafe to reach. Building schools, in other words, is necessary but not sufficient; governments must also train teachers, provide meals and support the families whose circumstances keep children away.

The report calls for stronger public investment and better data, and it insists that education is not merely a route to employment. It is a foundation for health, civic participation and equality, and a childhood without it is a loss that societies continue to feel for decades. The hardest cases are often the least visible ones: children with disabilities, those living in conflict zones, and those who work to support their families. If data does not count them, policy will not reach them, and children who miss school early rarely catch up later. Progress will not come from a single global summit but from sustained funding, safe schools and policies aimed at the children who are easiest to ignore, for every year a child spends out of school is a year of learning that cannot be fully recovered.

articles.title: The Digital Divide

More people are online than at any point in history, yet access remains strikingly uneven. The World Bank's digital progress report notes that billions still lack reliable internet, particularly in low-income countries and rural areas, and that even where coverage exists many people cannot afford a device or a data plan.

The divide, however, is not simply a matter of cables. Skills matter: a person who can send a message may still be unable to use online banking, apply for a job or check health information. Content matters as well, for where public services exist only in a dominant language, some groups are effectively excluded. Trust is a further barrier, especially in places where fraud and surveillance are common, since people who fear being cheated or watched will avoid the very services designed to help them. Even the design of a form or an application can exclude someone whose literacy is limited or whose connection is intermittent.

Governments can lower costs by encouraging competition and investing in public infrastructure, and schools and libraries can teach digital skills while providing access for those who have none. Regulation matters too, since a market dominated by a single operator rarely produces affordable prices. Services should be designed for people with low literacy and limited connectivity rather than for the already connected, whose habits are so often taken as the norm.

The goal is not to put every service online, which would merely penalise those least able to use it. It is to ensure that digital tools widen opportunity instead of creating a new hierarchy of insiders and outsiders. A connected society, after all, is not one in which everyone owns a phone; it is one in which everyone can use the connection to learn, work and be heard. Judged that way, digital progress looks less like a question of coverage and more like a question of who is genuinely able to take part.

articles.title: How to Read the News
articles.summary: 面对新闻，先看来源、日期和证据，再判断标题是否夸张。媒体素养不是记住结论，而是学会追问信息从哪里来。
articles.text:
News now arrives faster than judgement can follow. A headline appears on a phone, is forwarded through a group chat and repeated by people who have read no further, all before anyone has checked whether it is true. In such an environment media literacy is not a refinement for the educated; it is a basic skill of citizenship.

The first question to ask is deceptively simple: who published this? A familiar logo does not guarantee accuracy, but an unfamiliar site with no contact information and no named editor deserves caution. The second question concerns date, for an old story can be reshared as though it had just happened, and its age is often the detail most easily stripped away.

Next, look for evidence. Does the article name its sources? Does it link to a report, a court document or an interview? A headline may make a sweeping claim while the article beneath it rests on a small study or a single comment, and the gap between the two is where misunderstanding thrives. Statistics deserve particular care, since a percentage can convey urgency while concealing the size of the sample behind it. It is worth asking, too, what is missing: which voices were not consulted, which figures were left out, whose interests the framing happens to serve.

Good journalism does not pretend to be neutral about facts, but it should be fair about people and evidence, and readers can hold it to that standard. Media literacy, properly understood, does not mean distrusting everything, which is merely cynicism in another form. It means slowing down long enough to ask how we know what we think we know. The habit is cumulative, for each claim checked makes the next one easier to question, and a reader who is curious about how a story was made will carry that curiosity long after the story itself has been forgotten.

articles.title: What Museums Are For
articles.summary: 博物馆不只是保存物品，也承担教育、研究和社区服务。它们如何讲述历史，会影响公众如何看待自己和社会。

A museum is still often imagined as a quiet building full of old objects, visited on rainy afternoons and forgotten thereafter. In reality museums do many things at once: they collect, preserve, research and explain, and in doing so they choose what to display and, just as significantly, what to leave out.

Those choices matter far more than visitors tend to notice. An exhibition can make a group's history visible or render it invisible; it can present a difficult past as a reassuringly simple story, or it can invite visitors to ask hard questions for which no comfortable answer exists. Museums are not neutral mirrors held up to the world; they are places where people decide, deliberately or by default, what is worth remembering. Silence, too, is a form of statement, since what a gallery omits teaches visitors just as surely as what it displays.

Many museums are now changing in response. They work with communities to tell stories in unfamiliar ways, open spaces for discussion rather than merely for contemplation, and use digital tools to reach people who cannot visit in person. Some are rethinking how their objects were acquired and whether some of them should be returned, questions that touch on money, national pride and the legacies of empire and that cannot be settled by a single exhibition.

A good museum, then, does not only protect the past; it helps a society understand itself. That is why funding, access and honest interpretation are not secondary administrative issues but part of what makes a museum genuinely public, and why the composition of a museum's board, and the sources of its money, are not irrelevant to the story told inside. A museum that explains its choices invites trust, even when the story it tells is uncomfortable, whereas one that prefers silence may keep its objects safe and lose its audience.

articles.title: The Housing Squeeze
articles.summary: 住房越来越难负担，不只是房价问题。收入停滞、供应不足和金融政策共同作用，影响年轻人的独立、生育和城市活力。
articles.text:
In many cities housing has become the largest single item in a household budget. Rents and purchase prices have risen faster than wages, especially for young adults and low-income workers, and the resulting squeeze determines where people live, when they leave the family home and whether they can save at all.

The causes are complex and resist easy blame. In some places too few homes are built where people actually want to live; in others land is expensive, planning rules are restrictive and construction costs are high. Such rules, whatever their merits, often make it slow and costly to add homes where demand is greatest, while low interest rates made borrowing easier for a time but also pushed prices upwards. Investors searching for safe assets added further demand without adding a single bedroom.

The consequences extend well beyond money. Households that spend most of their income on rent save less, spend less in local shops and enjoy less freedom to change jobs, since moving may be impossible. Delayed independence affects family formation and mental health, and essential workers are increasingly priced out of the cities they serve, commuting for hours to teach, nurse or clean in places they cannot afford to inhabit. Such effects are cumulative, since a decade of high rents shapes a generation's sense of what a normal life should cost.

Solutions are not simple, and anyone offering a single remedy is probably selling something. Building more homes undoubtedly helps, yet secure tenancies, social housing and measures to stop speculation from crowding out residents help as well. A city that cannot house its workers is not a successful city; it is merely an expensive one. Housing is infrastructure, and when it fails the effects appear in health, education and work, which is why the debate is not really about whether housing matters but about who is willing to pay for the conditions that make it affordable.

articles.title: The Air We Breathe
articles.summary: 空气污染每年导致数百万人过早死亡。细颗粒物来自交通、工业和家庭燃料，减少污染需要交通、能源和城市规划共同行动。
articles.text:
Air pollution rarely announces itself. A sky of unbroken blue may still carry particles fine enough to slip past the body's defences, settle deep in the lungs and pass into the bloodstream, where their effects accumulate over years. The World Health Organization links such exposure to millions of premature deaths each year, through heart disease, stroke, lung cancer and a range of respiratory conditions. Because the damage is gradual and its sources are diffuse, the harm is easily treated as a background condition of urban life rather than as an emergency demanding a response.

The sources are familiar enough: traffic, industry, power plants, and the domestic burning of wood, coal or waste. In many cities the problem sharpens in winter, when heating demand rises and cold, still air traps pollutants near the ground, so that the same emissions do considerably more damage. Less often acknowledged is how unevenly that burden falls. Poorer neighbourhoods, frequently sited beside busy roads, freight depots or industrial zones, record the highest concentrations, while households with the means to move away breathe noticeably cleaner air.

The health consequences follow a similar pattern. Children, whose lungs are still developing, older people and those already living with illness are more vulnerable to the same dose of pollution, and outdoor workers - couriers, builders, street vendors - may have little practical choice but to breathe it for hours at a stretch. Reducing pollution is therefore not merely an environmental question. It is a question of health equity, since those who contribute least to emissions are often those who absorb most of them.

None of this is beyond remedy. Cleaner public transport, renewable energy, stricter vehicle standards and more green space all help, and so do policies that address the sources together rather than one at a time; a city that cleans up its cars while tolerating coal fires has solved only part of its problem. Measurement is a necessary beginning, but a city that monitors air quality and does nothing more is merely keeping a record of harm. Clean air is not a private choice. It is a shared condition, and it requires public action.

articles.title: Rules for AI
articles.summary: AI 伦理不只是技术问题，也涉及隐私、偏见、责任和人的尊严。原则需要变成法律、审计和可追究的实践。
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence now helps to rank job applicants, to recommend which medical tests a patient should undergo, to decide which comments remain visible online and to allocate public services. Such systems can be genuinely efficient, processing in seconds what would take a team of people weeks. They can also reproduce historical bias at scale, conceal the reasoning behind a decision and disperse responsibility so widely that no individual appears answerable for the outcome.

Fairness, transparency, accountability and human oversight recur in almost every set of ethical guidelines, and stating them is the easy part. The difficulty lies in translating them into working practice. A model that is accurate on average may still fail a minority group systematically, because the average conceals exactly the cases that matter most. A system that supplies an explanation may still leave an ordinary person without any realistic means of challenging the result, particularly when the reasoning is buried in a technical report that no one outside the company can interpret.

UNESCO's recommendation on the ethics of AI confronts this gap directly. It argues that regulation should protect human rights and dignity, and it calls for impact assessments before deployment, transparent data practices and remedies for people harmed by automated decisions. It is equally explicit about what should lie beyond the pale, warning against social scoring and mass surveillance - applications that turn a technology of prediction into an instrument of control.

Rules alone will not make a technology good, and anyone who imagines otherwise has not read much history. But without rules the costs fall on those with the least power to resist them. Regulation has to be clear enough to guide companies and flexible enough to adapt as the technology changes; a principle without a remedy is only a slogan, and the real test of AI ethics is what happens when something goes wrong. Artificial intelligence will shape society in any case. The question is who gets to decide how, and on whose terms.

articles.title: The Pet Effect
articles.summary: 养宠物可能带来陪伴、运动和责任感，也可能增加费用、过敏和压力。健康收益取决于生活方式和动物福利。
articles.text:
Pets are widely credited with improving health. Dog owners walk more, cat owners report company, and many people insist that their animals help them feel calm. The appeal of the idea is obvious: a simple, furry answer to loneliness and stress, available without a prescription.

The evidence, however, is mixed, and it is worth separating what studies show from what owners feel. Research suggests that dog walking can raise levels of physical activity, especially among older people for whom a daily walk is otherwise easy to postpone. Pets can impose routine and supply a reason to get up in the morning; for some people, caring for an animal lends structure and meaning to days that might otherwise blur together. These are real benefits, though they are difficult to measure and easy to overstate. Evidence for cats is thinner, resting largely on self-report, and much of what owners describe may owe as much to the comfort of routine as to the animal itself.

Yet a pet is not a universal medicine. Animals cost money, demand time and can provoke allergies or injuries; a badly matched pet may add stress rather than relieve it. For someone on a limited income or in unstable housing, the responsibility can quickly become overwhelming, and the animal suffers alongside the owner. Veterinary bills arrive without warning, and a rental contract may forbid pets altogether. The growing practice of prescribing pets for loneliness deserves scepticism precisely because the consequences of a poor match fall on both parties.

The lesson is not that pets are bad for us. It is that the relationship is what counts. A well-cared-for animal and a prepared owner may both benefit; an animal acquired as a quick fix for a human problem usually benefits neither. The sensible advice is unglamorous: choose carefully, plan for the cost, and take the animal's needs seriously as needs in their own right, not as a form of therapy that happens to be alive.

articles.title: More Than Plants and Soil

articles.text:
A community garden can look modest from the street: a few raised beds, a shed, a water butt and a group of neighbours who seem to spend a surprising amount of time standing around talking. Its social value may be far larger than its footprint suggests. Gardens give people a reason to meet, a pretext for conversation and a shared place to care for.

The benefits are easiest to see in those who are usually left out. For older residents, a garden supplies routine and company at an age when both can be scarce. For children, it may be the first occasion on which food is something grown rather than bought. For newcomers, it offers a way to meet people without needing flawless language, since much of the work can be demonstrated rather than explained. In practice the shared labour often matters more than the vegetables, which is why a poor harvest does not necessarily make a bad year.

None of this happens automatically. Community gardens can be exclusive in quiet ways. Plots may be expensive, waiting lists long and rules unclear; a garden controlled by the same small group for years can drift into becoming a private club, whatever its founding intentions. Good projects therefore share decisions, welcome beginners and keep access cheap, recognising that inclusion is a practice rather than a statement.

Cities can help by providing land, water and long-term security, since a garden on a site scheduled for development is hard to invest in. But no council can create one by decree. A garden needs residents willing to turn up in February as well as in July, to weed when nothing is flowering and to settle disagreements about compost. The best of them grow both plants and relationships, and it is the second harvest that is harder to measure.

articles.title: Wages Under Pressure
articles.summary: 工资增长放缓、生活成本上升，让许多家庭感到压力。生产率、谈判力量和政策支持决定工资能否跟上物价。
articles.text:
For many workers the past few years have felt like a race run without a finish line. Prices rose quickly and wages did not always keep pace; even where pay increased, housing, food and energy bills often increased faster. The result is a peculiar kind of fatigue, in which people are earning more on paper and feeling poorer in practice. A pay rise that is absorbed by rent is not, in any meaningful sense, a pay rise. Wage growth, after all, is not a single number but the outcome of several forces pulling in different directions.

Productivity is one of them. If workers produce more value per hour, there is more room to pay them more without simply pushing prices up. Bargaining power is another. Unions, labour shortages and minimum wage rules all influence how much of the value created ends up in wages rather than in profits, and the balance shifts with politics as much as with economics.

The picture varies sharply by sector and country. Some groups of workers have secured substantial increases; others, particularly those in low-paid and insecure jobs, have fallen further behind. Young people and new entrants to the labour market often face the greatest difficulty, since they lack the seniority and the fallback savings that make it possible to wait for a better offer. A single average wage figure can conceal all of this, which is why averages are so often quoted by those who benefit from them.

Policy can help, though it cannot conjure wage growth out of nothing. Investment in skills, enforcement of labour standards and support for collective bargaining all shape how gains are distributed. None of these levers works quickly, and several are easier to announce than to sustain. Inflation complicates the arithmetic further: a 4% rise when prices climb 5% is a cut in real terms, however welcome the headline figure looks. Beneath the technical arguments lies a larger question - whether an economy rewards work, and not only ownership.

A row of trees can change a street more than a new pavement does. On a hot day the shade they cast can lower the temperature enough to alter how people use a space: where they walk, where they linger, whether they stop to talk. Trees also absorb rainwater that would otherwise run into drains, shelter birds and insects, and give a neighbourhood a calmer, less exposed feeling.

Yet trees are still widely treated as decoration, a finishing touch added once the serious business of construction is done. A new building may include a few young trees, planted in soil too shallow and with no plan for watering, pruning or eventual replacement. Planting is visible and photographs well; maintenance is neither. Many saplings die within a few years, not because the species was wrong but because no one was responsible for them. Species are chosen for size and price rather than for tolerance of drought, and the soil provided is often too compacted for roots to spread.

Cities that value trees treat them as infrastructure, on a par with pipes and roads. They map their trees, set budgets for care, protect mature specimens during construction and plan replacements decades ahead. They also consider equity, because green space is unevenly distributed: wealthier neighbourhoods tend to have more of it, while poorer areas often have fewer trees, less shade and streets that are measurably hotter in summer.

Planting is a gift to the future, but a tree needs decades to become the tree that matters, and the interval between planting and benefit is exactly where political attention tends to lapse. A city that plants trees for a photograph is not the same as a city that plans for shade in twenty years. The real test is not the ceremony but the watering rota, the pruning budget and the willingness to protect a mature tree when a developer would rather remove it.

articles.title: The Password Problem

articles.text:
Passwords were designed to protect accounts, and in principle they do. In practice they have become a burden that users are expected to carry on behalf of systems that ought to protect them. Because few people can remember dozens of distinct passwords, many reuse the same one across services; a single leak then exposes several accounts at once, and the damage spreads far beyond the site that was originally breached, often surfacing months later.

Security experts recommend long, unique passwords for every service, which is sound advice and nearly impossible to follow unaided. Password managers can generate and store complex passwords, so that the user needs to remember only one master password, and two-factor authentication adds a further step, such as a code sent to a phone. Neither is glamorous, but together they remove much of the daily friction that leads people to take shortcuts.

Biometrics offer a different approach. Fingerprints and face recognition are convenient, always available and impossible to forget, which is precisely why they are spreading. They cannot, however, be changed if stolen, and a compromised fingerprint is compromised for life. They work best as one layer among several, not as a complete solution, and it is worth noticing how readily convenience is allowed to settle questions of security. The same convenience explains why so many systems still fall back on a password the moment a fingerprint fails to register.

The real problem is not only memory, nor even user negligence. It is the sheer number of accounts people are now expected to maintain and the way companies design security, often treating the user as an obstacle to be managed. Better systems would reduce the burden on users, detect unusual activity and make recovery simple rather than humiliating. Until those systems arrive, a password manager is a practical first step, and a reasonable rule is that a good system should make the secure choice the easy choice.
