Tourism can be a force for good. It creates jobs in places where steady employment is scarce, supports local businesses from guesthouses to taxi drivers, and gives visitors a direct encounter with cultures they would otherwise know only from screens. Few industries spread money so widely across a region, and few depend so heavily on the goodwill of the people who live there.

But when too many visitors arrive in the same place at the same time, the benefits can be outweighed by the costs. Overtourism is visible in crowded streets, rising rents and damaged landscapes; less visibly, it makes it harder for residents to afford housing or to use the public spaces that were theirs. A town can find itself unable to function for the people who keep it running all year. Some destinations have responded with visitor limits, tourist taxes and campaigns to spread arrivals across the seasons. Behind the crowds lies a quieter mechanism: when apartments are converted into short-term lets, the housing stock left to residents shrinks and rents climb.

Travellers can change their behaviour too, and often the most useful changes are the least dramatic. Visiting outside the peak season, staying longer in one place and spending money with local businesses all reduce pressure and spread income more evenly. Learning a few words of the local language, respecting rules about photography and treating sacred sites as places of worship rather than backdrops are small signs of respect that residents notice.

The goal is not to stop travelling, which would be neither realistic nor desirable. It is to travel in a way that does not make life worse for the people who live there. Tourism is not a right to enter someone else's home without consequences; it is a relationship that has to be negotiated, season after season, between guests who are temporary and hosts who are not. A good tourist remembers which of the two they are.

articles.title: The Vegetarian Burger
articles.summary: 植物肉被宣传为更环保的肉类替代品，但它的健康、价格和环境收益取决于生产方式。消费者需要看清标签，而不是只看广告。
articles.text:
Plant-based meat is sold as a solution to several problems at once: animal welfare, climate change and personal health. Burgers, sausages and nuggets made from plants now sit in supermarket chillers and on restaurant menus, and the marketing tends to be refreshingly simple - eat this instead of meat and the world will be better. The promise is attractive precisely because it asks so little of the consumer: a single swap appears to settle questions of ethics, climate and diet at once.

The reality is more complicated. Plant-based products generally use less land and water than beef, which is a genuine advantage, but processing and transport carry costs of their own, and the comparison depends on what is being replaced. Nor is the environmental case uniform: a product shipped long distances in refrigerated packaging may compare less favourably than its makers suggest. Their health profile varies widely: some are high in salt or saturated fat, others are fortified with vitamins, and a highly processed patty is not automatically healthier than a simple meal of beans and vegetables. The label "plant-based" describes an ingredient, not a nutritional guarantee.

Price is another barrier. Plant-based meat is often more expensive than the animal version, which limits who can buy it and turns a supposedly universal solution into a middle-class option. Taste and texture have improved considerably, but not every consumer is convinced, and habits formed over a lifetime rarely change simply because a product claims to be better.

The best choice therefore depends on the product and on the diet as a whole. Reading labels, eating more whole foods and reducing waste may matter more than switching to a single branded burger, however virtuous the packaging. A better food system will not be built by one product; it will be built by many choices about what we grow, what we buy and what we throw away.

articles.summary: 托育费用高，影响父母是否工作、生育和家庭收入。公共补贴、带薪假期和高质量托育能减轻负担，但需要长期投入。
articles.text:
Childcare is a practical necessity for most families, and in many countries it is priced like a luxury. The cost of a nursery place can swallow a large share of a parent's income, and for low-income households it may determine whether working is worth the effort at all. The calculation is rarely abstract: it is made at the kitchen table, with a calculator, at the point when a second child arrives or a promotion demands longer hours.

The consequences reach well beyond a household budget. High costs can push parents out of the labour market, and the parents most often pushed are mothers, who still carry most of the caring. A delayed return to work reduces lifetime earnings and pension contributions; the decision about whether to have another child may be shaped by the price of a place rather than by preference. Businesses lose skilled workers they have trained, and the economy loses productivity it can ill afford. Informal arrangements fill part of the gap, but they depend on grandparents who may live far away or be in work themselves.

Some countries respond with subsidised childcare, free hours for young children or tax credits; others invest in paid parental leave and flexible work. Design matters as much as spending. A subsidy that mainly benefits wealthy families, or a place that does not exist in the neighbourhood where it is needed, leaves the problem intact. Availability, affordability and quality have to move together, since any one of them alone solves little.

Quality deserves particular attention. Cheap childcare that is unsafe or unstable is not a real solution, and the staff who provide good care are themselves underpaid in most countries. Affordable, accessible, high-quality care is expensive, but so is the alternative of leaving parents without options. Childcare is infrastructure for the next generation, and treating it purely as a private expense is a choice with public consequences.

articles.title: How Reading Has Changed
articles.summary: 阅读没有消失，而是在改变。手机、有声书和短视频改变了注意力和阅读习惯，也带来新的读者和新的挑战。
articles.text:
Every few years the obituary of reading is written anew. The young, it is said, spend their evenings on phones, their attention broken into fragments, and the long, patient encounter with a book belongs to a world that has gone. The diagnosis is not baseless, but it is drawn from too narrow a sample. People have not stopped reading; they read in different ways, on different devices, and often for shorter stretches than their grandparents did.

Digital technology has widened access in ways that are easy to forget. A single e-reader can hold a library of thousands of volumes, allow a passage to be found in seconds and fit into the gaps of a commute. Audiobooks have opened books to commuters and to readers whose sight is failing, while online forums have revived the informal club in which readers argue, recommend and lend. Set against the conditions of a generation ago, the supply of words has grown rather than shrunk.

Access, however, is not absorption. A screen invites interruption: a notification arrives, a video promises something livelier, and the sustained concentration on which a long novel depends is exactly what such an environment erodes. Scrolling and reading are different habits, and the second is the harder to acquire because it must be practised against the grain of the device. It would be sentimental to pretend that nothing is lost.

The choice before us, then, is not between print and digital, a dispute that matters less than its partisans suppose, but between attention and distraction. Families can set aside an hour in which no device intrudes; schools and libraries can defend quiet as a condition of learning rather than an indulgence. The book survived radio, television and the internet, and it will probably survive the phone, provided we make room for it. That task belongs less to the next generation than to this one, and it rests on a modest recognition: reading is not a moral test but a form of attention, and attention, like any capacity, improves with practice.

articles.title: The Case for a Later Start
articles.summary: 青少年生物钟偏晚，太早开始上课可能影响睡眠和学习。推迟上学时间需要校车、课程和家庭安排配合，但可能值得尝试。
articles.text:
For as long as there have been secondary schools, there have been adolescents who arrive at them half asleep. Parents, understandably, read this as laziness, and many teenagers, having been told so often enough, are inclined to agree. The biology tells a different story. During adolescence the internal clock that governs sleepiness shifts later, so that a fifteen-year-old who must rise at seven may feel no drowsiness until well past midnight, however early the alarm is set.

A student who begins the day already in debt to sleep does not merely yawn through the first lesson. Attention, mood and memory all suffer, and the damage accumulates: sleep-deprived teenagers are more accident-prone and, over time, more vulnerable to a range of health problems that have little to do with diet or exercise.

Evidence from schools that have pushed back the first bell is cautiously encouraging. Attendance tends to improve, and concentration in early classes, particularly among the oldest pupils, appears to benefit. Yet a timetable is not a lever that can be pulled in isolation. Buses are contracted, sport and part-time work are arranged around existing hours, and parents' working days assume that children are occupied from eight until three. Reform, in other words, redistributes inconvenience before it distributes benefit, which is why so few schools attempt it.

Framed this way, the argument is not about indulging the young. It is about matching the school day to what is known about adolescent sleep, and about admitting that a timetable is never a neutral instrument: it announces what a school believes worth protecting, and one that begins before its pupils can reasonably be awake has quietly ranked convenience above learning. Moving the first bell by half an hour is a modest administrative act with effects that persist until the last lesson. Whether the adults who set the schedule will absorb the disruption is, in the end, a question about what they take sleep to be: a luxury, or a condition of thought.

articles.title: Strength Is for Every Age
articles.summary: 年龄增长会流失肌肉，但力量训练在任何年龄都有帮助。从轻重量、简单动作开始，能改善平衡、日常活动和独立生活。
articles.text:
Strength training is usually imagined to belong to young athletes, and the image is not entirely unfair: the sport of lifting is indeed young, loud and competitive. What the image conceals is that strength itself matters at every age, and that its gradual loss is one of the quieter costs of growing older. From about thirty, adults begin to shed muscle mass; the process accelerates later in life and makes itself felt in balance, in walking, in carrying shopping and in the simple business of rising from a chair.

Nor is a gym required. Body-weight exercises, resistance bands, bottles of water and flights of stairs all supply a challenge, and the principle is the same in each case: begin at a level that feels manageable and increase it slowly. Progression matters as much as the starting point, since the load must rise often enough to prompt adaptation yet gradually enough to be tolerated. What defeats most beginners is not laziness but impatience, the attempt to start where they hope to finish.

For older adults the returns are strikingly practical. Stronger legs reduce the risk of falls, which remain among the most serious hazards of later life; stronger arms make daily tasks less arduous; and training appears to support bone health and mood as well. Where health conditions complicate matters, a doctor or instructor can help to adapt the movements rather than abandon them.

Muscle loss, then, is not the inevitability that many people assume. It can be slowed and partly reversed, and while the earlier someone begins the better, it is never too late to start. Strength is not a luxury reserved for athletes but part of the infrastructure of independent living, and the best exercise is rarely the most sophisticated one; it is the one a person will actually keep doing, week after week, for years.

articles.title: The Garden in Your Head
articles.summary: 园艺不只是体力活动。接触土壤、观察植物生长和完成一件小事，能缓解压力，也能带来掌控感和成就感。

Gardening occupies an ambiguous place in the public imagination: a pastime for the retired, a luxury for those with land, a pleasant enough way to spend a Sunday. It is also, less obviously, a practical form of health care. Digging, planting and watering involve movement, fresh air and attention directed at something other than oneself, and each of these is in short supply in an ordinary indoor day. Few forms of exercise are as forgiving, moreover: a garden can be taken up in an afternoon and resumed after a fortnight without penalty.

Gardeners often describe a particular calm that descends while they work, and the explanation is probably twofold. Part of it is physical: moderate activity, sunlight and time outdoors are all associated with better mood and sleep. Part of it is mental. A garden sets small, clear tasks, and it returns visible evidence of effort, even if the evidence is only a bed cleared of weeds. Few other kinds of work offer feedback so immediate and so difficult to dispute.

None of this makes gardening a cure for serious mental illness, and it would be dishonest to present it as one. Nor is it equally available to everyone, since a garden of one's own depends on space, money and time that many people lack. A window box, a shared plot or a community garden can widen access considerably, and the point of such schemes is not to grow perfect vegetables but to spend time on something that grows.

There is also a lesson in the pace. In a world of screens and notifications, a garden demands a different quality of attention: slow, seasonal and not entirely under our control. That last feature may be the most valuable of all, for it teaches patience, the recognition that not everything can be rushed and that some goods arrive only to those who wait.

Amateur theatre invites comparison with its professional cousin, and the comparison is rarely flattering: the acting is less polished, the sets are simpler, the budgets are smaller and the reviews, such as they are, come from the audience rather than the press. Judged by these measures, amateur companies will always come second. Judged by what they actually do, the ranking looks rather different.

They give people the chance to perform, direct, design and organise, and in doing so they distribute, to people whose working lives offer little scope for either, skills that professional theatre mostly keeps to itself. For many participants the stage is a place to learn, to build confidence and to discover capacities they had not suspected. It is also a social world: rehearsals produce friendships as reliably as they produce scenes, and performances draw neighbours together in halls that are otherwise empty. A village hall, in a place that has lost its shops and its bus service, may be the only public building left, and filling it is no small service.

Amateur companies can tell local stories that professional ones ignore, and they can stage plays in village halls, schools and community centres, reaching audiences who rarely set foot in a city theatre. Tickets are affordable, the atmosphere informal, and the distance between performer and spectator small enough to be crossed in a conversation afterwards.

None of which means that quality is irrelevant. Amateur groups can be ambitious and exacting, and the best of them are. The argument is narrower: they should be judged by their own purposes rather than solely by professional standards, because culture is not a pyramid with a single peak but a network of places where people make things together. A stage does not have to be professional to be meaningful, and a community that makes its own culture need not wait for permission to begin.

articles.title: The Social Power of Laughter
articles.summary: 笑不只是对笑话的反应，也是一种社交信号。它能缓解紧张、拉近人与人之间的距离，并对身体产生轻微益处。
articles.text:
Laughter is normally explained as a response to something funny, and the explanation is only half right. People laugh far more in the company of others than they do alone, and much of that laughter follows no joke at all. It arrives at the end of a sentence, in the pause after a mistake, or when a conversation has become unexpectedly awkward, which suggests that it is doing social work rather than merely registering amusement.

Researchers who study the behaviour describe two functions. Laughter eases tension, and it signals to those present that a situation is safe, that no offence has been taken and that the group can relax. A shared laugh can make a difficult conversation feel less threatening, and it can bind a group together at precisely the moments when its members are tired or nervous. In this respect it resembles a small, wordless form of reassurance.

The physical effects are more modest than the popular press suggests. Laughter relaxes muscles and alters breathing, and some studies associate it with reduced stress, but the evidence is not strong enough to call it a treatment, still less a substitute for medical care. Claims that it cures illness belong to advertising rather than to science, and the honest position is that the benefits are real but limited.

The practical lesson is not that jokes should be forced into every room, which would be exhausting and probably counterproductive. It is that laughter depends on company and on comfort, and that both can be cultivated. A workplace or classroom where people can laugh together is often one where they can also think and disagree, because the laughter has established that disagreement is not dangerous. People wait until the flat is tidy, the cooking impressive and the space adequate, and since those conditions rarely coincide, the party is postponed indefinitely. A good party need not be perfect; it needs to be warm, regular and open, and a little effort of this kind can produce a surprising quantity of connection. Part of the explanation is economic. When AI lowers the cost of producing a draft, a report or a piece of code, organisations rarely respond by producing the same amount and banking the difference. They demand more. A task that once consumed a day is now completed in an hour, and the hour that is saved is promptly colonised by requests that were previously too expensive to make. Efficiency, in other words, does not automatically convert into leisure; it converts into throughput unless something else intervenes.

Monitoring compounds the effect. Some employers use these tools to track activity, count keystrokes or score performance, and workers who know themselves to be measured tend to compete with the measurement, even where the metric bears little relation to good work. Nor is measurement neutral: a metric designed to make work visible tends to reward what is countable rather than what is valuable. The result is a paradox: a technology introduced to remove tedium generates a new species of anxiety, and the anxiety is itself productive of hours.

The promise of a shorter week, then, is not self-fulfilling. Whether productivity gains become time depends on how those gains are distributed. If output rises while wages and hours remain fixed, the benefit accrues elsewhere, and the tool that saved time merely raises expectations about how much work is possible. A shorter week has to be decided upon, negotiated, legislated or bargained for, and no upgrade, however capable, will decide it on our behalf.

articles.title: Sharks and the Limits of Marine Parks

A recent survey of shark populations suggests that the reality is more stubborn. Some parks have recorded genuine recoveries; others, apparently similar in design, have recorded almost nothing. That divergence is the interesting finding, for it suggests that protection is not a single intervention but a set of practices whose results differ widely.

Two variables explain much of the difference. The first is enforcement. A boundary that is not patrolled is a line on a chart, and fishing that continues unpunished inside a reserve produces much the same outcome as fishing outside it. The second is scale. Sharks reproduce slowly and range widely, so a protected zone may cover only a fraction of an animal's life, sheltering it during one season and releasing it into unprotected water the next. The two interact: a large reserve that is not enforced offers little, and a small one that is enforced offers less than its advocates hope.

What happens beyond the boundary matters as much as what happens within it. Sharks that swim out can still be caught; coastal development, pollution and warming water impose stresses that no designation can exclude; and a park that safeguards a reef while ignoring the current that feeds it protects an island of habitat in a deteriorating sea.

The lesson is not that marine parks fail, but that boundaries are a beginning rather than an achievement. Effective protection demands funding, sustained monitoring, the support of the communities that fish and depend on these waters, and cooperation among the jurisdictions between which mobile species travel. Conservation, on this view, is a practice rather than a designation: something that must be paid for, staffed and defended long after the announcement has been made. None of this is an argument against parks, only against treating a designation as an accomplishment.

California contains some of the most expensive housing in the United States, and for decades the standard explanation has been restrictive zoning, the rules that cap how many dwellings may stand on a given plot of land. The consequence, critics argue, is an artificial scarcity that bids prices upward, generation after generation.

Recent reforms have set out to test that explanation. Some laws permit denser apartment buildings near transit stops and job centres; others ease the conversion of commercial premises into homes, or allow small additional units in back gardens. The common thread is a deliberate increase in supply where demand is strongest, on the theory that adding homes in desirable places does more good than adding them in remote ones. Whether such a strategy can lower prices, or merely slow their rise, is disputed even among economists who support it.

Supporters concede that results will be gradual. Construction is slow, costs remain high, and a law passed this year cannot house a family next year; even optimists expect the effect to arrive slowly, if it arrives at all. Critics raise objections of a different kind: that new building accelerates neighbourhood change, displaces the tenants it is meant to serve, and produces units too expensive for low-income households. Market-rate construction alone, they contend, cannot solve a problem that afflicts precisely those least able to pay.

Beneath the technical disputes lies a question about obligation, about what a city owes the people who live in it. Supply matters, but so do rent protections, social housing and public investment, none of which follows automatically from a changed zoning code. California's experiment is therefore best understood not as an answer but as a test: of whether rules can be rewritten quickly enough to matter, and of whether a market can be made to serve more than those who already hold its rewards.

Labour is scarce, materials are costly and permits move slowly, and families spend the interval in temporary accommodation. In response, some communities have turned to modular construction: buildings manufactured in sections in a factory and assembled on site. The sections arrive largely complete and are lifted into place.

Advocates point to two advantages. Factory conditions make the process predictable, since weather and site delays intrude less; and because sections can be produced while the ground is prepared, site work and manufacturing proceed in parallel rather than in sequence. Waste falls too when materials are cut in a controlled setting, and precision manufacturing can improve quality, since a factory jig holds tolerances that a windy site does not. For a family waiting for a permanent home, such gains are not abstractions.

Yet modular housing is no simple remedy. Local codes may fail to recognise factory-built dwellings, and mortgage lenders, unsure how to value them, may hesitate. Oversized sections travel awkwardly on narrow roads, design choices can be constrained by what a lorry can carry, and some buyers suspect that anything assembled quickly will feel provisional. Each obstacle is institutional rather than technical, which makes it no less binding.

The real test is whether modular construction can be absorbed into a long-term housing strategy rather than reserved for emergencies. Should codes, finance and design adapt, it offers one credible route to more homes; should it remain a niche, it will rescue some families while leaving the wider shortage untouched. It is not a substitute for the labour, materials and land that housing still requires, nor can it make land available or shorten the queue of families waiting for it. Speed, after all, matters most to the household that has been waiting, not to the industry that builds.

Nor is it confined to a single stream: similar discolouration has appeared across the region, which makes a purely local explanation unlikely.

Permafrost is ground that stays frozen through most of the year, and it acts as a vault. Minerals locked in that frozen soil remain immobile for as long as the ground holds; when it thaws, they become mobile. Iron oxidises and stains the water, while other substances raise its acidity. The consequences travel through the food web, reaching fish, insects and the people who depend on these waters for food and livelihood.

The orange rivers are valuable precisely because they make visible a process that is otherwise difficult to perceive. Climate change is habitually measured in degrees, yet its effects surface in soil, water and ecosystems, and not always gradually. Some changes accumulate quietly; others cross a threshold and become difficult, perhaps impossible, to reverse. A river integrates everything upstream of it, which is why it records change so faithfully and why that record is so easy to overlook.

The extent of the problem is still being established, and honesty requires saying so. What is already clear is that monitoring is not a luxury. A river that changes colour issues a warning, but only the underlying chemistry can indicate how serious the change is, how far it may spread and what might reasonably happen next. Without such measurement, the phenomenon remains a spectacle, striking to look at and impossible to interpret.

Consistency across a department matters too, since a rule that differs from seminar to seminar teaches students that rules are arbitrary. Compacted soil, drought and a lack of watering during the first summers account for many losses, and none of these attracts much attention. Many trees die long before reaching the size at which their shade would matter.

Cities that take trees seriously plan on a scale of decades. They select species suited to the local climate rather than to a catalogue, protect mature trees that cannot be replaced within a generation, and budget for maintenance as they would for any other piece of infrastructure. The exchange is unequal: felling a mature tree and planting a sapling are not equivalents. Residents have a part to play as well, watering in dry spells, reporting damage, and arguing for trees when a pavement is widened or a site redeveloped.

The benefits of a large tree cannot be accelerated, and this is what makes the canopy a test of civic patience. A city that plants for a photograph is not the same as one that plants for shade in twenty years, and the difference will be visible long after the officials who chose have left office. The Arctic is warming faster than almost anywhere else on Earth, and one of the consequences is buried in its ground. Much of that ground has been frozen for millennia, preserving the remains of ancient plants and animals in a vast reservoir of carbon. While it stays frozen, that carbon is effectively locked away. When the ground thaws, microbes begin to break the material down, and in doing so release carbon dioxide and methane into the atmosphere.

The process is gradual, which is precisely what makes it easy to underestimate. Methane is a far more powerful greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide over the short term, and the additional emissions it represents feed back into the warming that caused the thaw in the first place: a loop in which the Arctic, long treated as a passive victim of climate change, becomes an active contributor to it. The uncertainty lies less in whether this will happen than in how quickly it will unfold, and in how much of the stored carbon escapes as methane rather than as carbon dioxide. No single year looks dramatic; the cumulative effect is of a different order entirely.

Thawing ground is also a physical problem for the people who live on it. Roads buckle, buildings subside and pipelines deform as the frozen foundation beneath them softens, and repairs in remote regions are slow and expensive. For communities already coping with high costs and thin infrastructure, everyday life becomes harder in ways that distant observers seldom see. Scientists therefore monitor permafrost closely, measuring how quickly it is changing and where the greatest risks lie, while local communities need support to adapt, whether through safer infrastructure or new ways of managing land.

None of this alters the fundamental arithmetic. Reducing global emissions remains the main way to limit the risk, because the thaw responds to temperature and temperature responds to emissions. The Arctic may feel remote, but it belongs to the same climate system that governs weather, sea level and food production elsewhere. What happens there does not stay there.

articles.title: The Politics of Food

Hunger is usually imagined as a distant problem, a matter of failed harvests in faraway places. In reality, food insecurity is a feature of rich countries too, and it is not always caused by a shortage of food. People go hungry because food is unaffordable, because work is unstable and income arrives unpredictably, or because social support is too weak to absorb a shock such as illness or a rise in rent. In such cases the shelves are full; what has failed is access.

Food banks and emergency aid matter, and it would be cynical to pretend otherwise. They carry families through a crisis that might otherwise become a catastrophe. But they are not a long-term solution, and treating them as one quietly shifts responsibility from public provision to private charity. What families need is stable income, housing they can afford and dependable access to healthy food, conditions that no donation can create. Schools and health services have a part to play as well, since a child who has not eaten cannot concentrate and a patient discharged into hunger will soon return.

The paradox at the centre of the issue is that food is wasted on an enormous scale while people go hungry. Shops discard unsold products, households buy more than they use, and edible food is thrown away because a date on a label has been misread. Better distribution, clearer labelling and communal meals can reduce that waste and widen access at the same time, though none of them explains why so many people cannot afford to buy food in the first place.

The deeper question, then, is political. A society that treats food as a basic right will make different choices from one that treats it purely as a commodity: it will regulate prices, protect incomes and accept obligations that no market can enforce on its own. Hunger is not a natural disaster. It is usually the consequence of decisions, and decisions can always be made differently.

Students also need to be taught how to use such tools critically: to verify a claim, to notice a bias, to recognise the difference between fluent prose and sound reasoning, and to explain honestly which part of a piece of work is their own. A school that ignores the technology altogether may send students into the world unprepared for it; a school that adopts it without reflection may weaken the very learning it exists to protect. Homes are larger, so a person can pass an evening without ever entering a shared room; shopping is online; work can be done remotely; entertainment arrives on demand and asks nothing of anyone else. Each of these conveniences removes a small obligation, whether to leave the house, to wait in a queue or to greet a neighbour, and the cumulative effect is a life that can be conducted almost entirely in private.

For some people this is a genuine gain, a release from noise and from company that was never freely chosen. For others it hardens into isolation. Social contact that once happened by accident now has to be arranged, and friendship demands an effort that busy schedules rarely accommodate, so the invitations go unsent and the drift goes unnoticed until it is well advanced.

Loneliness, moreover, is not merely a private feeling. It is associated with poorer health, lower trust and weaker communities, and its effects are not evenly distributed. People who are isolated often find it difficult to ask for help, while neighbourhoods with fewer shared spaces find it difficult to notice that help is needed. Nor is this simply a matter of willpower, since the ordinary infrastructure of a week now offers fewer occasions on which strangers are obliged to become acquaintances. A problem of this kind cannot be solved by telling individuals to be more sociable, because it is not, at bottom, an individual failing.

The answer is not to romanticise the past, which was hardly a paradise of belonging for everyone. It is to design for connection: public spaces that welcome lingering, community institutions with somewhere to meet, neighbourhoods that mix rather than segregate, and rituals that give people a reason to appear. Sleep advice is everywhere, and much of it sounds sensible. Get eight hours. Go to bed early. If you cannot sleep, stay in bed until you do. Have a glass of wine to relax. Catch up at the weekend. For people with occasional bad nights, such rules may do no harm. For people with insomnia, they can become part of the problem.

One difficulty is the number eight. Sleep needs vary with age, health and individual biology, and treating one figure as a target can create anxiety. A person who wakes at four in the morning may lie still, checking the clock and calculating how many hours remain. The calculation makes sleep less likely. The bed also becomes a place of frustration rather than rest.

Alcohol is another misleading remedy. It can make a person feel sleepy, but it disturbs the second half of the night and reduces sleep quality. Nor is it wise to spend hours in bed awake; experts often advise getting up after a period of sleeplessness and doing something quiet until tiredness returns.

The common thread is control. Insomnia feeds on effort: the harder a person tries to force sleep, the more alert the mind becomes. Good advice aims to reduce that pressure, not add another rule. Regular wake times, less light and caffeine late in the day, and a calm routine are more useful than a rigid target. None of this means that sleep hygiene is useless. Regular routines and a dark, quiet room can help. The problem is the promise of a single fix, and the blame that follows when it fails. Sleep is not a task to be completed by willpower.

Food waste is often imagined as a problem of careless shoppers. The reality is more structural. European households throw away a significant share of the food they buy, and the reasons begin before the shopping trip. Supermarkets encourage bulk purchases and two-for-one offers. Date labels can be confusing, especially when a product is still edible after its "best before" date. Busy households buy for an imagined week and then eat out, order in or change plans.

The environmental cost is serious. When food decomposes in landfill, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. The resources used to grow, transport and package the food are wasted as well: water, land, fuel and labour. Preventing waste is therefore better than recycling it, because the damage has already happened by the time scraps reach a bin.

Some solutions are simple. Planning meals, checking what is already in the kitchen and buying smaller amounts can help. So can understanding the difference between "use by" and "best before" dates. Retailers can reduce waste by selling imperfect produce, offering smaller portions and redesigning promotions that reward volume over need.

But individual habits are not enough. If shops treat waste as a marketing problem and households treat it as a personal failure, the system remains unchanged. The most effective approaches combine clearer labels, better storage, community sharing and rules that make producers and retailers responsible for what they create. Waste also has a social dimension. In many households, buying extra food is a way of showing care, preparing for guests or avoiding the shame of an empty fridge. These habits are not irrational; they reflect expectations about hospitality and abundance. A campaign that simply tells people to buy less may miss that emotional logic. Food waste is a daily habit, but it is also a design problem.

options: Confusing date labels and bulk promotions.

articles.title: How Urban Trees Cool Cities
articles.summary: 城市通常比周边乡村更热，树木通过遮阴和蒸腾降温；但树不是万能方案，缺水、空间不足和树种单一都会限制效果。
articles.text:
Cities are usually hotter than the countryside around them. Asphalt, concrete and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Cars, air conditioners and crowded buildings add more warmth. The result is an urban heat island, a pattern that can make summer dangerous for older people, outdoor workers and anyone without reliable cooling.

Trees help in two ways. Their leaves block direct sunlight, so the ground and walls beneath them stay cooler. They also release water vapour through their leaves, a process called transpiration, which cools the air around them. A well-planted street can feel several degrees cooler than a bare one, and the effect is strongest when trees are mature enough to create a continuous canopy.

Trees are not a simple fix. They need water, soil and space, and young trees take years to provide shade. Species must suit the local climate; a tree that survives drought may be different from one that grows quickly. Planting in the wrong place can damage pavements or conflict with pipes and wires. And trees cannot compensate for a city that continues to build heat-absorbing surfaces everywhere.

The most effective approach combines trees with other measures: lighter roofs, shaded bus stops, open water, ventilation corridors and buildings designed to reduce heat. Trees are living infrastructure, not decoration. Tree planting is also a question of justice. Wealthier neighbourhoods often have more canopy and more private gardens, while poorer areas may have more asphalt and less shade. A programme that plants trees without maintaining them can reproduce the same inequality in a greener form. They work best when a city plans for their roots, their water and their long life, rather than planting them as a quick symbolic gesture. Shade is not a luxury; it is basic infrastructure.

questions.q: How do trees cool cities?
options: By providing shade and releasing water vapour.
questions.explain: 第二段说树叶遮阴，并通过蒸腾释放水汽降温。

questions.q: Why are trees not a complete solution?
options: They need water, space and time, and cannot offset all heat.
questions.explain: 第三段说树需要水、土壤、空间，成熟需要时间，且不能抵消城市继续制造的热。

articles.title: Microplastics Are in More Foods Than You Think
articles.summary: 微塑料不只存在于海鲜；瓶装水、盐、茶包和加工食品都可能带来暴露。完全避免很难，但可以减少不必要的塑料接触。
articles.text:
Microplastics are tiny pieces of plastic, often smaller than a grain of rice. They have been found in oceans, rivers, soil and air, and increasingly in the food people eat. Seafood is the best-known source, but it is not the only one. Bottled water, salt, tea bags, canned food and processed products can all carry small amounts of plastic.

The health effects are still being studied. Researchers know that some particles can pass through the body, and that very small pieces may enter cells. What this means for long-term health is not yet clear, and scientists are careful not to overstate the evidence. The uncertainty is itself a reason to reduce unnecessary exposure, especially for children and pregnant women.

Some practical steps are simple. Drinking tap water from a glass or metal bottle avoids the plastic lining of many bottles. Avoid heating food in plastic containers, because heat can increase the release of particles. Choose loose tea or paper tea bags rather than plastic-based ones. Rinse canned beans and vegetables. These actions do not make food perfectly plastic-free, but they reduce one route of exposure.

The larger solution is systemic. Food packaging, water systems and waste management all determine how much plastic enters the environment. Individual choices matter, but they cannot replace regulation. The goal is not to frighten people away from eating fish or drinking water. Microplastics are also an environmental justice issue. Communities with unreliable tap water may depend on bottled water, and workers in informal waste systems are exposed to plastic dust and fumes. The people with the least choice often carry the highest exposure. It is to treat plastic as a material with a cost, and to use it only where it is truly needed. That is a public health question, not only a lifestyle choice.

questions.q: Which foods can contain microplastics?
options: Seafood, bottled water, salt and processed foods.
questions.explain: 第一段说海鲜最出名，但瓶装水、盐、茶包、罐头和加工食品也可能有微塑料。

questions.q: What is a practical way to reduce exposure?
options: Avoid heating food in plastic containers.
questions.explain: 第三段说不要用塑料容器加热食物，热量会增加颗粒释放。

articles.title: The Myth of Effortless AI at Work
articles.summary: 一项魁北克调查发现，“AI 会自然让工作更轻松”的说法站不住脚：节省的时间分布不均，验证与返工常被忽略，受益者往往是本就资源更多的人。
articles.text:
The promise of artificial intelligence at work is often told as a simple story: tools take over boring tasks, employees save time, and organisations become more productive. A major survey in Quebec suggests that the reality is more uneven. Workers do use AI, but the time they save is not distributed equally, and the work of checking, correcting and integrating machine output is often invisible in productivity estimates.

One problem is task structure. AI may draft a document quickly, but someone still has to decide what the document should say, verify facts, adjust tone and take responsibility for the result. For experienced workers, these steps can be fast; for novices, they may take longer than doing the task without AI. The technology shifts the location of effort rather than removing it.

A second problem is inequality. Workers with more autonomy, better training and stronger digital skills are more likely to use AI in ways that genuinely help. Those in routine jobs may receive tools designed to monitor or speed them up, with little say in how the tools are used. The result can be a wider gap between those who direct the technology and those who are directed by it.

The survey's lesson is not that AI is useless. It is that "augmented work" does not happen automatically. Organizations need to measure the whole workflow, train people to judge machine output and give workers a voice in design. The survey also complicates the idea of productivity itself. A task that takes less time is not automatically better if the result is less reliable or if the worker has lost the chance to learn. Speed is easy to measure; judgement, trust and skill are not. Without those conditions, the promised time savings can become another layer of unpaid labour.

options: They are uneven and often hide verification work.
questions.explain: 第一段说节省的时间分布不均，检查、修正、整合机器输出的工作常被忽略。

questions.q: Why can AI widen inequality?
options: Better-resourced workers can use it more effectively and have more control.
It is only available to managers.
It refuses to work for some people.
questions.explain: 第三段说资源、培训、数字技能更强的人更能从中受益，而常规岗位可能只得到监控/加速工具。

articles.title: Remote Work and the New Shape of Office Talk
articles.summary: 远程办公没有简单消灭同事交流，而是改变了它：视频会议可能让人更坦率，但非正式互动减少，团队需要重新设计沟通方式。
articles.text:
Remote work was expected to make colleagues more distant. In some ways it did: hallway conversations disappeared, and the small exchanges that build trust became harder to schedule. But research on remote teams suggests a more complicated picture. When people meet through video, some conversations become more open, not less. The screen can create a sense of permission, especially when the topic is difficult.

The change is not evenly positive. Informal communication is where much workplace knowledge travels: who is struggling, which project is stuck, what a manager really means. Remote teams often replace this with scheduled meetings, which are more efficient on paper but less spontaneous. New employees suffer most, because they cannot learn by overhearing.

The design of the tools matters. A team that uses video only for formal updates may become colder; a team that leaves time for casual check-ins, small groups and open channels may become closer. The medium does not determine the culture. The habits built around it do.

The office was never only a place for tasks. It was also a stage for belonging, rivalry, mentorship and luck. Remote work removes some of that stage and replaces it with a different set of signals. The lesson for organizations is that remote work is not a switch between "office" and "home". It is a redesign of how attention, trust and information move. The best hybrid arrangements do not try to reproduce the old office exactly. Remote work also changes power. A manager who cannot see a team may rely more on written updates, and written updates favour people who express themselves well on paper. Quieter employees can become less visible, while those who speak easily in meetings gain more influence. The office had its own biases; the screen has different ones. They ask which conversations need a room, which need a screen, and which need no agenda at all.

options: Some conversations become more open on video.

questions.q: Who suffers most from lost informal communication?
options: New employees who cannot learn by overhearing.

articles.title: Space Junk and the Cost of Rescue
articles.summary: 地球轨道上的碎片越来越多，卫星碰撞风险上升；救援卫星比想象中困难，追踪、避碰和移除碎片都需要国际合作。
articles.text:
Space near Earth is becoming crowded. Satellites provide navigation, weather data, communications and scientific observations, but they share orbit with spent rocket stages, broken parts and fragments from past collisions. Even a small piece of debris can cause serious damage at orbital speed. The problem is not only the number of objects but the difficulty of predicting where they will be.

Rescuing a satellite is harder than it looks. A servicing spacecraft must match the target's orbit, approach safely and avoid creating new debris. The window for action may be short, and the cost is high. When a satellite fails, the choice may be between an expensive rescue and losing the service entirely. A growing debris population makes both options more urgent and more risky.

Tracking is the first defence. Operators need to know when a collision is possible and who should move. That requires shared data, agreed rules and systems that work across countries and companies. Removing debris is harder still: nets, harpoons, lasers and robotic arms have been proposed, but each raises questions about cost, liability and who is responsible for cleaning up.

The deeper issue is governance. Orbit is a shared resource, and no single country owns it. Without coordination, the incentives point toward launching more and cleaning up less. Space junk is often described as a technical problem, but it is also a collective-action problem. Orbit is also an economic space. Insurance, launch licences and access to scarce slots all depend on reliable information about what is up there. A collision does not only destroy a satellite; it can create thousands of fragments and make an orbit less usable for everyone. The technology exists; the harder task is agreeing on how to use it before the next collision makes the choice for us.

options: It requires matching orbits, safe approach and avoiding new debris.
There is no way to track satellites.

questions.q: What is the deeper problem behind space junk?
options: It is a shared resource requiring international coordination.
questions.explain: 最后一段说轨道是共享资源，没有单一国家拥有，缺乏协调会导致发射多、清理少。

articles.title: Chatbots, Privacy and the Limits of Consent
articles.summary: 聊天机器人会收集大量个人数据；仅靠“同意”条款无法保护用户，因为人们很少理解数据如何被使用，法律需要更明确的透明度和责任。
articles.text:
Chatbots feel like conversations, which is part of their appeal. A user types a question, receives an answer and may share personal details without thinking of the exchange as data collection. But every message can be stored, analysed and used to improve a model. The informal style of the interaction can make the privacy risks harder to see.

Consent is the usual answer. privacy policies ask users to agree, and the agreement is meant to legitimise the processing. In practice, few people read the policy, and fewer understand how their words may be combined with other data. Consent also struggles with context: a person may be willing to share a health question with a chatbot but not with advertisers, employers or governments.

Regulation is beginning to address the gap. Proposals in several countries would require clearer information about what data is collected, stronger limits on sensitive information and more responsibility for companies that deploy chatbots. The details matter. A rule that only requires another pop-up may add inconvenience without adding protection. A rule that requires real choices, independent audits and penalties for misuse can change behaviour.

The challenge is not to stop people from using useful tools. It is to make the terms of the conversation honest. A chatbot should not feel like a private friend if it is also a data pipeline. Users need to know what they are giving, and companies need to be accountable for what they do with it. Privacy is not only an individual matter. When millions of conversations are collected, the patterns can reveal health trends, political views or financial stress at a population level. A single message may seem harmless; the aggregate is valuable. Without that, the friendliness of the interface becomes a form of concealment. That is the real risk.

questions.q: Why are chatbot privacy risks easy to miss?
options: The conversational style makes data collection feel informal.
questions.explain: 第一段说聊天像对话，用户容易忘记自己在提供数据，非正式风格让风险不易察觉。

questions.q: What does the article say about consent?
options: It is often not enough because people rarely understand how data is used.
questions.explain: 第二段说很少有人读政策，也不理解数据如何被组合使用，同意在语境上也有问题。
